MR. LLOYD JONES' REPLY TO
MR, FREDERIC HARRISON.
CO-OPERATION.
Mn. HARRISON does not sustain his objec-
tions to co-operation. What he has to say is
nearly altogether directed against the assump-
tions and methods of action adopted by cer-
tain of its friends. The co-operative idea, never-
theless, may be of the very first importance
by its truth and its saving power in a social
and industrial sense, and yet not an uni-
versal "panacea," as some of its over •zealous
friends may suppose; but the pillar of Simeon
Stylites does not discredit the Christian faith,
and so long as zealots abound in the world every
creed, religious, political, and social, must be
weighted by a certain number of them, and if
Mr. HARRISON finds himself in whatever faiths
he has accepted without such an embarrassing
companionship he has good reason to consider
himself lucky,
It is right to admit also that Mr. HARRISON'S
statement as to productive co-operation being
more difficult than distributive is true, but it
is a truth which co-operators as a body always
understood and acknowledged, and which,
whenever they attempt a practical experiment,
will force itself on their attention; but it is right
to inform him that even the productive side
of co-operation has been successful in a con-
siderable numb,?r of cases, and that in certain
of these a proportion of the profit is paid as
bonus on wages. It is true that taking
the whole profit as interest on capital is the
most general mode of proceeding, but even'
that, much as it may be condemned, is but an
experiment which may help in the future
establishment of the higher and better prac-
tice. It may be added that Mr. BRIGGS' plan,
though not co-operative in the sense in which
our oldest and most earnest co-operators
understand the idea, is yet a stop in the right
direction, and as such is to be encouraged in
the hope that it will, as it goes on, transform
itself into something more in accordance
with the true co-operative faith. In such a
work as co-operative production it is our duty
to welcome every well-meant effort, as each
may develop some point in its working useful
in its practical establishment. There is
room enough for the largest charity in the
practice of the co-operative movement, and for
the most encouraging hope that out of even
those diversities we now most suspect, we may
arrive at a unity in which all will believe and
on which all will rely.
I pass from those things, however, to assure
Mr. HARRISON that he depreciates unduly the
distribution side of co-operation. It is all that
he declares it to be, and much more, as it not
only liberates the worker from dishonest
trading, but it places in his hands the pecu-
niary means of doing anything he possesses
the intelligence and skill to do for his emanci-
pation as a worker from the thraldom of
capital. It gives working men the habit of
acting together in associative business—not a
small gain to men much of whose past suffer-
ings and misfortunes are due to isolation and
the distrust it breeds. And surely when Mr.
HARRISON tells us that, "if every worker and
labourer in England was a co-operator, that is,

No. V.

OUR ARISTOCRACY.-PRIMOGENITURE.

THE question as to the value of an aristo-
cracy will, during the next decade, receive
much discussion amongst the working men of
England. The treatment of almost every
new question shows the necessity of this. If
the people look for a higher degree of political
justice—our aristocracy stop the way. If they
demand laws which shall more equitably regu-
late the distribution of wealth—the same im-
pediment lies across the path. If we demand
a fuller competency for public office—actual
possession by an incompetent class discounten-
ances :the demand. If the evils of poverty
have to be provided against by legislation—the
rights of our propertied and!privileged classes
interfere to prevent it being done. Mot thus
at every step, frustrated at almost every point,
men are now beginning to inquire how this
aristocratic power has grown, by what props
it is upheld, what good and what evil it pro-
motes by its influence and its action?
The nation asks for a general system of
sound education, and the nobility and gentry,
countenanced and aided it by the Church—an
institution in near cousinship to our aristo-
cratic orders—make the carrying out of any
such system utterly impossible unless they can
mix some degree of profitable darkness with
the . light which education and knowledge
would bring. Better dwellings and superior
conditions of life generally, are required by
our tillers of the soil, but these are and will
be delayed to the point of revolution, lest our
privileged orders should find their profits, their
position, or their pleasures trenched upon.
Practically, society must either consent to
become stationary, to abandon the perform-
ance of all pressing obvious duties, or it must
demand from these impeding obstructive per-
sonages by what patent held from GOD or man
they put themselves above right, above law,
above public convenience—above all, those
considerations by which individuals and
societies of men preserve their lives, increase
their happiness, or by which the progress of
peoples in liberty and civilisation is secured.
How aristocracies or privileged classes have
come to us, and how they are perpetuated, we
know almost as well as we know where plague
or pestilence first came from, and how they
are best encouraged. We can study aristo-
cracy in the old world—in India, Ethiopia,
Egypt, Greece, and Rome—and in these an-
cient States, where we see it rampant, we see
the people perish in its shade ! If we study
it in modern history It exhibits the same spec-
tacle, and carries with it the same lesson;
only modern history offers some few instances
of the re-invigoration of national life by partial
checks given to its dangerous overgrowths.

the old. Feudalism resting on landed pos-
sessions has now to struggle with a new
wealth, and a new intelligence, created by
industry and. art, and in this struggle I doubt
not that side will win which aims at realizing
for the general public the largest amount of
moral and material good. Looking at the
growth of our great families, we cannot help
seeing that the nation has been beggared for
the advantage of those who—swell out as they
may—never can be anything but a class. Let
the working men of England take into their
minds a few facts, sal from these draw their
own conclusions. Ido not wish to write long
expositions of the laws of Primogeniture and
entail, but now that the pretensions of pro-
perty are becoming arrogant beyond endur-
ance, and more and more arrogant by the
mere fact of enlarged and enlarging posses-
sions, I wish to state plainly that in one
hundred years, or thereabouts, the actual pos-
sessors of the soil qf England have been reduced
in number to about one-eighth—in other words,
seven-eighths of' the old proprietors have been
squeezed out. Nationality is thus sinking into
proprietorship, and what a man possesses, and
not what he is as a citizen, is becoming every
day more and more the measure of his worth.
At the very root of this is the law of
Primogeniture. It begins in the family what
is aggravated and encouraged in the nation.
It disinherits the many that the one may be
aggrandized. It strips the younger branches
of a family that the eldest may have all;
and thus sanctions and justifies the beggary of
the many that the few may wallow in an use-
less and unuseable abundance. This one law
by which the eldest robs the youngest in a
family is a pure iniquity which ought to be
dealt with, without needless delay; as whilst
it gives to the fortunate first-born the shares
of the unfortunate later-born, it puts upon the
parents the duty of plundering the public in
every possible way, that the family injustice
may as far as possible be compensated at the
expense of the nation.
It would be worth reckoning up—if any of
our statists would take upon himself the task,
of finding out—how much of our Church
revenues have been sucked in to fill the purses
of those left bare by this abominable law.
Or it would be interesting to know how much
the hardworking people of England have been
defrauded by means of pensions granted on the
most frivolous pretexts, and salaries or sinecure
offices where the duties were little more than
a knavish pretence. I say nothing now of
naval and military expenses, a large proportion
of which wero neither more nor less than fees
for the disinherited junior branches of our
aristocratic families. Millions upon millions
have thus annually been absorbed, and other
.millions every year to pay for the pauperism
and misery caused by this atrocious system!
This drainage of the country's revenues,
though somewhat contracted, goes on still.
When will the stern voice of the people de-
clare with unmistakable emphasis that it shall
flow no longer, and insist upon the stoppage
of the injustice that keeps it flowing; or
when will men freely thrust their hands
amongst the dusty records, which tell plainly
the conditions upon which the aristocracy
of England hold their lands, and which will
inform us plainly also how far they fulfil the
obligations imposed upon them by their
tenure?

ia devising an,y plan for the purpose Of taking

First let me say, however, that the " Com-

TUE DOITIME-SIIIFT SYSTEM.

On this question I must also take the
liberty of putting aside minor considerations,
that I may at once get to the heart of the
difference between Mr. HARRISON and myself.
The only real question is whether the
"double-shift system" be possible in our
leading industries where expensive machinery
is extensively used, as if the proposal break
down here, it fails to satisfy the purpose for
which it WAS suggested. "In grand forms
of industry," says Mr. HARRISON, "when
works are entirely produced under time con-
traots, and the organization is on the grandest
and oompletest scale, the double-shift system
- seems singularly fit. Whenever, or wherever,
the short hours of human labour neutralize
the economy of machinery, the answer is
simple adopt the double-shift system.
Wherever it is applioable an immense saving
at once arises. The work of the machine
would be increased 60 per cent., and produc-
tion would be increased 60 per cent., for the
works would be active sixteen hours instead
often." _ .

I need scarcely say here that unless there
be an increased production the system is of no
use; whilst if there were a suddenly expanded
power of production it would be injurious,
unless there was a corresponding and con-
tinuous expansion of demand; and as ts 60
per cent. being an over-estimate of increase,
against which Mr. HARRISON feels called on
to protest and argue, I have only to point to
the quotation given above from the Fortnightly
to show that the estimate is Mr. IlAunisores,
not mine, and that in proving "assumption un.
sound," he is impugning his own statement, and
not a statement put forward by me. What I
am responsible for is the assertion that two
shifts in our factories and great workshops
would involve two sets of hands of equal
number, that is a doubling of the employed
people.; and it is difficult to see how this can
be gainsaid.

Mr. ThinursoN's plan of meeting my objec-
tions by limiting the number of workshops
and. quantity of machinery in operation, looks
like an attempt to get rid of one difficulty by
creating another. How is the proposed limita-
tion to be effected? Are numbers of those in
business to be asked to withdraw, or are persons
who may contemplate going into business to be
kept out? Is a man already engaged in manu-
facturing likely to give up that those who
remain may have a chance of putting the
double-shift system in practice that they may
derive a profit from it? Or are those who
eontemplate going into business to be denied
the right to do so that the new scheme may
have a better chance of success? Borne expla-
nation not yet given is needed here, as all past
experience warrants the belief that rival em-
ployers are far more likely to increase than to
diminish in numbers.

But supposing all such difficulties done
away with as may suggest themselves in con-
neetion with the working of this system, and
they are very numerous, it would be the duty
of the working men to oppose it at every step
of its progress. Under certain circumstances
working men no doubt prefer large employers
to small ones. In certain senses they are
preferable, but that a system should be
encouraged by which the whole of the country's
business should be thrown into the hands of
such persons is quite another matter, and
requires many points to be considered beyond
mere minor matters of convenience. It would
not be good for the working men to have all
business placed in the hands of such industrial
eo/essi. Since the commencement of the pre-
sent century hundreds of thousands have
escaped from the worst drudgeries of labour
into comfort sad independence; and, although

rlarge numbers of those have not made the
best use of their new power and position, yet
all hope would die out of the worker's heart if
this road was dosed, and the means of escape
absolutely cut off. Had this plan been tried
with success at the time mentioned, we should
now have a set not of millionaires but of billion-
aires, who could drive back every poor fellow
attempting to escape from the workshops ; and
even groups of workers as ca-operators could
be and would be hopelessly crushed down, as
we saw, even as things are, in the case of the
Wolverhampton look-makers—by all power-
ful eapital insatiably hungry for profits, and
capable of punishing any attempt made to
share them. What has hitherto been done by
individuals for the purpose of bettering their
condition, and what our co-operators are now
trying to do by association would inevitably
become a hopeless work in the presence of such
adversaries. In fad, our employers and our
workers under such a system would become
two distinct castes, the one elevated and the
other degraded, without any hope from that
social interfusion which now keeps alive in us
those ideas of a common humanity and a com-
mon interest in justice which are our strongest
aids in our progress in civilization.
These objections are not urged in any spirit
of opposition to Mr. MASSEY Or Mr. HARRISON.
Mr. BRASSEY'S book, in which the suggestion
of a double-shift is to be found, is the most
honest work yet published from the employer's
Bide on the labour question; whilst Mr.
fLinnisorr, who advocates the idea, has always
proved himself a friendly and powerful
auxiliary on the side of our workers. Both
are entitled to the highest respect, but on this
subject they are, I venture to say, both mis-
taken; and there cannot, I think, be much
doubt that the operatives of England will so
consider them, amongst whom at the present
moment there is a strong dislike of the double-
shift system wherever it exists. They do not
sigh for powerful masters; their desire is to
be masters over themselves. They are
yearning for deliverance, not for servitude;
for escape from a crushing competition, not to
remain on the low ground of competition
where they are too frequently ruined. by its
intensity. They are listening for the eo-ope-
tive voice that shall say to them, like that
heard before the final fall of Jerusalem,
"Let us depart hence."

LLOYD JONES:

TRADES UNIONISM OUR FOREIGN
TRADE AND TUE FREE BREAK-
FAST TABLE.

Tin grand mistake and the root of all the
evil of trades unionism lies in the fact, that
it is based upon antagonism between employer
and employed, whose interests are (when
properly understood) identical and mutual.
Being based upon this unsound foundation,
the effect of all their efforts must neeessarily be
partial and limited as regards the apparent
good results, whereas the evil effects are un -
told and unlimited.

Unhappily the former is seen and felt by the
parties interested; but the latter is unseen
until it is too late to save society from the con-
sequences.

A,Tr. ALFRED A. WALTON baB taken to
criticising Mr. Baraes's paper, which appeared
in these columns on the 12th inst.

But with all due deference we think Mr
W4i,Tox rather to wordy, i.e., more words are
used than are necessary to state the ease.
Mr. BRIGGS would be glad to enter into a
friendly controversy on the question of trades
unionism, but one article in a newspaper does
not afford the time and. space to answer all
the points in detail. The gist of the whole
question is this, viz., that whilst society is
engaged in a death struggle about wages,
our (so called) rulers are engaged in making
Treaties of Commerce which bind. the masses
of the people (on both sides) to action, which,
in the nature of things, tend to destroy their
trade and put society into this fix, viz., that
whilst a very few may get richer the in asse
are left out in the cold, getting poorer and
poorer. This is the inevitable result of all
fiscal systems which put a tax on the trans .
actions of the people; and this alone is what
prevents the law of supply and demand havin g
a fair trial,

Trades unions need not necessarily be that
unmitigated evil that people are wont to call
them, if they would but lay aside that bitter-
ness of feeling between employer and employed,
and join hands with them, and go at once for
" free breakfast table." Mr. BRIGGS has
seen some of the workings of trades unions for
the last forty or fifty years in different capaci-
ties. First as an apprentice, then as a
journeyman and trades unionist, then as an
employer, and this is the school of experience
in which he was taught—not as a middle man,
but one who had really to battle with the
realities of life—the fact regarding the weak
and the strong being put on a dead level as
regard wages. It would be too long a story
to go through the whole history of this
checkered life in the limits of these columns,
and not necessary for our purpose.
Mr. WALTON says, "I rather suspect that
Mr. BRIGGS is one of those whose fear is that
higher wages are detrimental to the trade
commerce and industry of the country."
Nothing could be further from the truth. On
the contrary, he is of opinion that, if the bur-
dens imposed on industry by our fiscal system
were removed entirely, the increase of our trade
would be of a more healthy character; coal,
iron, and machinery would perhaps not be ex-
ported to such a vast extent, but our export
trade in our legitimate and natural productions,
such as manufactures, foreign and colonial
produce, and agricultural implements, bitter
beer, tto., would grow and increase steadily,
and profits and wages would grow together in
such a way as to make a bond of peace
between employers and employed, and
moreover, the distribution of wealth would be
by a self-acting process more just, more equal,
and more blessed in every way. The old
nursery proverb that, " GOD never sends
mouths without sending meat to fill them,
or backs without clothing, or providing
means by which they may clothe themselves"
would be a fact accomplished. Trades unions
would then have little difficulty in coming to
terms with their employers, as was the case
from the time the Corn Laws were repealed
until 1866, when Black Friday made it evi-
dent that the cotton famine, added to the fiscal
laws, had shaken the industry of the whole
empire.

What is the use of boasting of our increase
in trade if none but coal and iron get any profit
out of it?

I can give instances of more than one firm
who had almost doubled their returns in the
turnover last year, but whose net profits were
less by half what they used to be in former
years. These are not the two branches (coal
and iron) which Mr. NV4LTorr has selected
(very unfairly we think) as an illustration of
the prosperity of the ganeral trade of the
country. And this we do not attribute to the
action of trades unions so muoli as to that fiscal
system which prevents the natural growth of
commerce throughout the whole habitable
globe.

Look at our international exhibitions; con-
sider tho efforts of our enterprising men who
for gain (and very properly so) are racking
their brains to encircle the globe with an iron
band; our great inventors and civil engineers,
who are bringing out almost daily some means
by which GOD'S people, from pole to pole, may
the more eadly be brought into peaceful com-
mercial intercourse. Consider how their pro-
gress is impeded and the ends of peaceful
science and art frustrated by those mischievous
fiscal obstructions. It would seem that the
legislative mind is the only mind that stagnates
and sticks in the mud of petty local and
frivolous party and personal questions.

Mr. WALTON says, that " in fact, many of
the leading trades unionists have for years
been working hard for fiscal reform and a free
breakfast table, and are prepared to work on
till that be accomplished."
Again, as if he would rather they would not
meddle with the "free breakfast table "
question, ho says, " Mr. BRIGGS must knew
that trades unions are not political organiza-
tions, nor are they fiscal or financial reform
associations, although nearly all their leaders
are very able, political, fiscal, and financial
Wormers."
There would seem to be a contradiction in
terms in the aboye two quotations. The

word "many" would appear to need some
explanation; amt again, if they have been
working for years, we should kindly request
Mr. WALTON to explain how it is they have
done so to so little purpose, seeing that half
the duty on coffee was all that we could
squeeze out of Mr. LOWE last Session; whilst
the American Government has abolished at
one stroke the entire duties on sugar, tea,
and coffee, thereby giving their agriculture
and manufacture a great advantage in the
race of competition with us in the markets
of the world. Great as is the wickedness of
the American Government in this cursed pro-
tective system, there seems to be hopes in this
abolition, as a beginning, that they are be-
ginning to go a-head in the right direction,
and will take the wind out of the sails of JOIIN
Bum. in financial reform, as they have done
in that of Waste Land Laws and diplomacy.
Let us advise Mr. WALTON and the trades
unionsists in general;to consider that they have
now gained victory enough over capital, for a
while at least, and that there is a vast amount of
misery amongst unskilled agricultural labourers,
in numbers about five to one of trades
unionists, whose cause require investigation,
and grievances, which if not soon redressed,
will ere long break forth like a volcano, spread-
ing devastation and death everywhere. It
would be madness to expect this mass—dis-
persed over the soil so sparsely as they are—
to effect any good by strikes, &o.
Would it not be more conducive to the
happiness of all, if all capitalists and la-
bourers, both skilled and unskilled—as in the
case of repeal of the Corn Laws—were to lay
aside their bickerings about wages, &0., and
also all political party spirit—for a "Free
Breakfast Table " knows no political party,
or religious creed? therefore, all parties may
consistently stand on one common platform,
advocating a cause, which, in the nature of
things, must tend to promote the greatest
happiness for the greatest number.

Trades unions would then prove that they
were above selfishness or self-seeking pro-
clivities. They would then see that what is
good for each is good for all, and what is good
for all is good, for each.

One word about the Labour Representation
League. The word " league " once had a
meaning—when it was an Anti-Corn Law
League—but then it had at its back both
labour and capital everywhere ; one hundred
thousand pounds and the unanimous voice of
the people, marching in procession with their
flags embellished v. ith peace-emblems, were
vastly more powerful for good than anything
that the present generation of leagues and
societies have so far proved themselves to be.
Why has not a working man's representative
turned up at all and every one of the recent
elections ? It does not follow that men

shall all be required to come from the ranks of
labour direst, in order to represent the masses.
Let the masses put forward their wants anti
desires in no unoertain sound that they must
have "the Bill, the whole Bill, and nothing
but the Bill," viz., "the Free Breakfast Table,"
and we will warrant advocates in the Houses.
" Great is truth, and it will prevail."

When shall we be able, on a Free Breakfast

Table,

articles.title: GIBRALTAR.
articles.text:
GIBRALTAR.

IN the BEE-HIVE of February 17th, while
advocating the giving up of Gibraltar to
Spain, I wrote as follows I venture to
prophecy that the time is close at hand when
a formal demand will be made for its restora-
tion. Would the working classes of this
countty allow a war to be carried on in such a
cause? I trust not. Then, if the occupation
is such that it cannot be rightly defended by
a war, it ought not to continue."
It was, thou, with great interest that I read.
the following telegram front Madrid, in the
Times of October 21:—

-
"In to-day's sittings of the Congress a de-
puty presented a petition requesting the
Government to commence negotiations With
Great Britain respecting the cession of the
fortress of Gibraltar to spain."

And it was With no less interest that I found
upon another page of the same paper a leading
article on the subject. For when the Times
thinks it necessary to have a leading article in
defence of our occupation of Gibraltar, it
shows that the opposite opinion and the
Spanish demand. have a certain strength. And
when I had read the article, I considered that
the Times had, in spite of itself, done good
service, and materially advanced the opinions
which it denounced. As was to be expected,
the Times ridiculed. the notion of our ceding
Gibraltar, offering the usual reasons which are
current among our commercial and military
classes, and which it sums up thus :—" What
we have to say upon this view of the question
Is short and simple. Gibraltar cannot be
given up." An argument always used to jus-
tify the continuance of political crimes, It is
the common practice of our rulers to exagge-
rate the difficulties and inconveniences which
must necessarily occur whenever we resolve
not to perpetuate iniquities which we have
been committing. When we strike at the root
of a bad policy, and endeavour to substitute a
better policy, founded upon a higher morality,
of course there are political difficulties, which
demand wisdom and skill on the part of our
political servants. But our so-called states-
men always make out that the difficulties are
too great, until the time comes, and when they
find that their places and power depend upon
their dealing with these questions, and then
they find that, after all, the difficulties may
be overcome by their own wonderful states-
manship I

The article in the Times is, however
a very good article. It shows that our
government of Gibraltar has been of the
very worst description, that its occupa-
tion by the English has, in fact, been
a nuisance and grievance to the Spanish
people. This is a valuable admission, and I
subjoin an extract from the article. But in
doing so, I would remind working men that
the crime of our misgovernment is altogether
different from that one of holding Gibraltar.
• Reform of this misgovernment might be
desirable ; but that is not the question.
Sooner or later we must restore Gibraltar to
Spain, and if we do not do it voluntarily, we
shall some day be compelled to do so. It can
never be tolerated in civilized; Europe, that
one nation should hold a fortress in the middle
of another country, or that one nation should
possess an impregnable fortress on the coast of
another country. Our holding Gibraltar is a
constant menace; to Spain, and outrages the
proper. national feeling of every Spaniard,
worthy of the name. I was told, when I
wrote on this subject before, that the cession
•of Gibraltar involved :the cession of all our
possessions. Among others Hong Kong was
specified. I have Written six articles on China,
and showed that it is not so—that the Chines*
questions have nothing to do with the cession
of Hong Kong. Each of these grave questions
of International policy has to be determined
upon its own merits. And while it is per-
fectly true that the same principles of morality
must govern all cases, it is not true the same
solution is common to them all. I am well
aware that this. not a complete reply to the
objections to which I allude ; that underneath
these ,commercial and military views, there
lurk conceptions as to our imperial policy,
from which I dissent, and which I entirely
repudiate, but which nevertheless deserve a
fuller discussion than I can at present give to
them. I shall hope to revert to this topic upon
some other occasion. The notions which have
hitherto prevailed, whether of military glory,
or of the forcible extension of our trade by
means of war, are already beginning to create
disgust. Our commercial classes and our
soldiers must ho taught that there is a rapid
change going on; that day by day we are be-
coming more resolved that the selfishness of
strength and power shall be curbed and ground
down, by a higher and mightier force, that of
the evergrowing moral nature of mankind.
Our aim now is to change, by moralising our
national conduct, to substitute for the old
vices ef forcible supremacy, military glory and
national aggrandisement, a nobler international
policy, founded upon the duty which we owe
to other peoples and to the human race.

HENRY. CUOMPION.

STAFFORDSHIRE.

THE coLLlans AND IRONWOREERS.

Whilst throughout East Worcestershire most
of the notices of engine minders for a rise of Is.
a day in their wages and a reduction of our hour
per day as the working period, together with the
notice of the masters that the men should leave
their employment, terminated on Saturday night,
throughout the Wolverhampton and Elston and
Willenhall districts of South Staffordshire the
notices on each side will come into operation
next Saturday. Throughout the Wednesbury and
the Hill-top and Goldshill districts, however, the
notices, like those relating to East Worcestershire,
terminated on Saturday; and ae the men showed
no disposition to yield their principle, masters
followed the course pursued by the leading em-
ployers about Dudley—they ordered the horses to
be brought out of the pits, and arrangements for
the stopping of the furnaces also.
The precise demand of the engine tenders may
be no great matter, but its success, they add,
means also tho success of the colliers, who are
agitating for a rise of 15 per cent. The men on
their part complain that their masters have been,
and still are, getting unexampled prices; that
wages have been much under the proportion they
should bear to prices, and that when they seek to
interview their masters, accompanied with their
agents, they are denied an audience.

WOOLWICH.
THE WOREMEN AT THE ROYAL ARSENAL.

The long-expected decision of the Secretary of
State for War upon the memorial of the Royal
Arsenal workmen has been received, and was
published to the workmen in the several depart-
ments on Monday morning, in the following
order: "The workmen in this department are
hereby informed that the Secretary of State has
been pleased to sanction a reduction of the working
hours (from the 4th November) from fifty-six to
fifty-four per week, without any corresponding
reduction in the daily rates. While making this
concession the Secretary of State has been further I
pleased to direct that the privileges hitherto en-
joyed by the arsenal workmen shall not be in any
way curtailed; and when the great advantages of
four and a half days' holiday with pay per year,
sick pay, and gratuitous medical attendance,
together with full pay when suffering from
accident, are considered, it is hoped that the
consideration thus shown towards the men by the
Government will lead to increased activity and
zeal on the part of all those who are fortunate
enough to be employed in the public service. It
is understood that the reduction will be effected
by the men leaving off work at half-past five
instead of six o'clock on the first four days of the
week, working until six on Fridays as usual.

WOLVERHAMPTON.
THE BRABSWORRERS.
The brassworkers of Wolverhampton resolved
to give a week's notice to-day (Saturday), to leave
the employ of all masters in the trade who do not
give the 15 par cent. advance recently granted to
the brassworkers in Birmingham.

CARDIFF.
THB SOUTH WALES COAL TRADE.

There is a crisis impending in the house-coal
trade of South Wales. The men have for some
time been agitating for an advance of fourpence
per ton upon the present rate paid. On the Ist
October they gave notice that unless the demand
was conceded they would strike. On Wednesday
a conference took place at Cardiff between the
house-coal colliery proprietors and the representa-
tives of the men who desired to effect a compromise
by reducing their claim to twopence per ton. The-
masters stated that in view of a falling market
they would not make any concession, but offered to
submit the question in dispute to arbitration.
The delegates refused the suggestion of a reference.
The notices expirei on Friday, the Ist instant.
There are about six thousand colliers in the house.

articles.text:
THE AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF
CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

The
,dispute between the London and Man-
chester sections of the Amalgamated Society of
Carpenters and Joiners, which affected the in-
tereats of some 13,000 numbers, and funds to the
amount of about £20,000, was on Wednesday
brought to a satisfactory tennination. In May;
1871, the executive council of the bociety seized
the books and properly of the scciety, took_thera

&tun the house of Mr. Applegatth, the then
secretary, in Stumford-street, and established
themselves at East Temple-chambers, Whitefriars-
street. Mr. Applegarth protested, and the pro-
vincial portion of the general council, endorsing
his views, elected an executive council of their
own, having head•quarters in Manchester. A case
brought before Mr. Mansfield at Marlborough-
street Police-court, to test the legality of the
Manchester council's position, was dismissed, on
the ground that the society, being in restraint of
trade, was beyond the pale of the law. Both
parties then went before Mr. Stephenson, the
Registrar, who refused to register either society in
the original name until compelled by a mandamus
to do so. Then the London Council applied to
-the Court of Queen's Bench for a rule calling
upon the Registrar to register the society; but
the rule was
.refused on the ground that a Court
of Equity was the proper tribunal. At length,
after trying Police-court, Registrar, and Queen's
Bench, the parties turned their attention to
arbitration, and accordingly, at the end of
September, delegates from both sections met and
agreed that the whole question in dispute, viz.,
which section was entitled to the title and the
control of the funds of the society, should be
referred to arbitration. The arbitrators appointed
were Mr. John Kane, Secretary to the Iron
Workers' Society, Darlington; Mr. D. Guile,
Secretary to the Iron Founders' Society, London ;
Mr. Robert Austin, Secretary to the Engineers'
Society, Manchester; Mr. W. nicking, of the
G. U. of Carpenters, Nottingham; and Mr. George
Odger, London. These sat at the Bell, Old Bailey
for eight days. The business was carried on with-
out any legal assistance. Mr. T. D. Prior, the
Manchester secretary, represented his party, and
Mr. W. Harry, the secretary of the London section,
conducted the business on their behalf. Mr. Guile
was voted to the chair, and at the outset told his
brother arbitrators that their object was to adjust
the points at issue between the two societies, upon
terms such as they themselves, were the case
their own, would feel satisfied to accept. Some
dozen witnesses were examined. Those examined
by Mr. Prior wore cross-examined by Mr. Harry,
and vice-verstt, both being working men. Affi-
davits were put in, read, and marked, with all the
formality and certainly the decorum of a court of
law. During the eight days the work was har-
moniously carried on.
The unanimous award of the arbitrators was that
the title of Amalgamated Society of' Carpenters and
joiners should be conferred upon the Manchester
section, and that the locked-up funds of two
branches—Hoxton and Poplar—should be equally
divided between the two sections. The arbitrators
passed a resolution strougly urging both parties to
re-u nite.

to us, we have taken the above from the Daily
News of Wednesday.]

articles.text:
THE LONDON GASMEN.

On Wednesday evenhig a crowded meeting of
the gas stokers and others connected with the
London gas trade was held at the Cambridge Hall,
Newman•street, Oxford-street, under the presi-
dency of Mr. Lloyd Jones, to endeavour, if
possible, to abolish Sunday labour in the trade, and
to better their condition generally. The large
room was crowded to'excess. The Amalgamated
Gasmen's Association was represented in great
force, headed by a banner.
The chairman, in opening the meeting, said he
believed the object of the meeting—the abolition of
Sunday labour in the trade—was right and jast,
and he trusted their desire would be gratified. At
the present timepvery one had been asking fur
an improved condition of things. The persons
connected with gas works, who were there as-
sembled, if he was informed rightly, worked in
alternate shifts of 12 hours, and that went on from
one year's end to another; that on Sunday there
was no rest for the men any more than on a
Monday or any other day. They were, therefore,
the exception to the general rule with every trade
with which he was acquainted; that Sunday was
the day of rest, and it was a day of rest for all
labour, in fact, that was not absolutely necessary
for carrying on the business of society. He did
not put it on religious grounds .at all, but upon
the ground of necessity of rest from constant
labour on the part of men, of whatever occupation ;
and so strongly and universally had that been
felt that there was no country or religion in the
world that had not made provision of periodical
rest from the ordinary labour of life. They had
a right to put their claim ha of all others who were
engaged in earning their living by their labour.
They had a right to say to the public that unless
it was an absolute neoessity, they ought not to
eall upon men to give that day to lobour which

the rest of the world devoted to rest. ile believed
they had no disposition to strike, and concluded
by entreating the meeting to conduct all their
business with the greatest moderation, and he hoped
sincerely that they would get their reasotable
demands.

Mr. Webster then moved the following resolu-
lon :

That this meeting of the gasworkers of London
is of opinion that the time has arrived when they
should make a determined effort for the complete
abolition of Sunday labour, when such abolition is
practicable, and that this meeting is also of opinion
that there should be a rate of pay fixed at the rate
of time and a half for Sunday labour when the
abolition is impracticable.
Mr. G. Barker seconded the resolution, which
was put and carried unanimously, and the meeting
closed with a cordial vote of thanks to the chair-
man.

On Tuesday evening a meeting of the members

advisability of applying to the employers of the
trade to concede the nine hour system, as it is

trades.

that if it was asked for in a dignified and respect-

spontaneously, and that it was his opinion that the
employers did not wish to keep their employees
behind the men of other trailes, in respect to the
hours of labour or other ptivileges enjoyed by
them.

After some remarks from Messy. Britton,
honour, Nunn, Buck, and Wilson, to the same
effect, it was unanimously resolved that steps be
taken to further the movement; also a committee
was appointed, representing the various shops in
the trade, to organize an aggregate meeting of the
members of it, and to carry out the object
throughout the trade generally, with power to add
to their number from members of the trade present
at the said meeting. .

After 80M0 further conversation upon the sub-
ject, the members separated, highly satisfied with
the justice of their claim, and the belief that it
would be generally granted by the employers when
asked for it by the trade generally, upon a fair re-
presentation being laid before them.

On Monday forencon representatives from the
more important of the various mining districts in
Scotland met in Whyte's Temperance Hotel,

minors of his district to send a representative to

Association at Durham.

sentation of a testimonial to Mr. Wflonahl on

articles.title: STATE OP GIBRALTAR.
articles.text:
THE STATE OP GIBRALTAR.

The following is the extract from the Times
alluded to in Mr. Crompton's article :—lt would '
almost seem as if the system now in vogue were
devised with an object the very reverse of this—
that is to say, to make our occupation of Gibraltar
as annoying as possible to Spain. Gibraltar Is
not merely a strong citadel and watch post at the
mouth of the Mediterranean; it is a smuggling
station, mean and paltry in its gains, while to
Spain vexatious and costly. The old trade
theories which Lord Chatham favoured seem to
have been maintained at Gibraltar by oversight
and through ignorance rather than by design.
Everything is apparently designed so as to make
Gibraltar the entrepot whence goods may be smug-
gled across to Spain at every opportunity. Take
a single example, perhaps the most striking,
but still fairly characteristic of the rest of the
system. The importation and manufacture
of tobacco in Gibraltar are absolutely free. We
do not know that this can be said of any other part
of the world; it certainly cannot be said of any
other part of Europe, or of any of the countries
and colonies settled by Europeans. Why does
Gibraltar possess this singular immunity? It has
been preserved because it exists; but there can be
no doubt that it was originally established in order
that Gibraltar might be the mart for smuggling
tobacco into Spain. The result is that Gibraltar
may be described as a vast tobacco store. Every
other house is a tobacco warehouse. If you pass
an open doorway and see people at work within,
for a certainty they are making cigars or cutting
up tobacco and rolling up cigarettes. The ways
by which tho tobacco gets into Spain are innumer.
able. There are greardacostas and cruisers on the
look out; but if the virtue of the guardacostas is

proof against the constant temptations to conni-
vaLce presented to them, they are much
maligned. The truth is that everybody who
comes and goes is more or less a smuggler.
The Spaniards smoke more habitually than
any other nation of Europe, the Germans not
excepted, and the market is constantly active.
The man who brings ',vegetables and fruit across
the Lines, or fish across the Bay, to supply the
inhabitants., of the Rock, carries back a good part
of the price of his produce in tobacco. A beggar
whose rags seem scarcely to hold together has
tobacco wrapped up among his tatters. The !low-
ing sash of the Andalusian is an elastio pouch;
the cap of the Gitano is a storehouse. Infinite
ingenuity is spent in stowing away the contraband
article. And what is thus done on a small scale
is done also on a larger scale. There is scamely
a cove between Tarifa and Malaga which is not
the landing-place of fisher-smugglers, whence
cargoes are run up the mountains and conveyed
on mules into the interior.

It may be owned that we are not bound by our
occupation of Gibraltar to bolster up the revenue
system of Spain, but it is an unjustifiable abuse
of our position to make the place a nest of smug-
glers, causing annoyance and expense to the
Spanish Government. It is unjustifiable, and it is
unwise.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
Sui,—For some time past gentlemen have
been engaged in advocating the cause of the
claims of the agricultural labourer, and while
doing BO and urging the men to unite in one
common brotherhood (in union), they have in
their zeal designated the employers oppressors,
and some of us were inclined to think this
language rather severe and premature. But I
am sorry to hear that the agitators were not
out in their reckoning, for this week the wife
Of one of those victims has told me that her
husband was told by his employer, a Mr. 8.,
in the parish of Surfleet, not to come on his
land again, and also has received notice to
q_uit his (the employer's) house in duo course.
No doubt agreements only save this man
from ;immediate ejection ' • and this poor
man, just falling ill, applied to a class of gen-
tlemen who are expected to administer relief
to the necessitous, without respect to the appli-
cant's religious or social right of union. But
not so; he was branded with this fact, that he
was a member of the Labourer's Union, and I
believe if my memory serves me right, that he
was referred to the said Union for support
(contempt of course). I have also been in-
formed that a farmer residing in Holbeaoh
Drove, a Mr. J., has locked out one of his men
because he has come forward like a man of
principle, and joined.the Spalding League; he
also told him to go to Mr. GI-. M. Ball for a
winter's work, as he is one of his followers. I
maintain, Mr. Editor, that if the man has
hitherto been loyal to his employer, and. has
given no other cause to his master than the one
named for a discharge, the sooner such crea-
tures haste to the laud of Nod, and there
perish in obsourity, the better. Then, say they,
we have the poor at heart (but bettor rendered
at their feet), and we will, if loft to our better
judgment, elevate them. We will better
house them, better clothe them, and better
feed them. If the gentlemen referred to be a
fair specimen of that philanthropic class of
people, the less notice the poor man takes of
their canting the better. The simple fact is
this, they object to union, which is strength;
and many of them will profess anything to
accomplish their own purpose.—Yours truly,
Spalding. FAIR PLAY.

NEW TREATY OF COMMERCE WITH

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sia,—lt is a monstrous injustice, that of the

merce without consulting the House of Com-
mons. From what has oozed out already we

THE MEETING AT THE BELL INN ON
ELECTORAL REFORM.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
". SlR,—The purport of a speech, reported in
your last number, makes me utter, at the Bell
Inn, Old Bailey, on the 22nd inst., what
rather surprises me.
I am made to say a further extension of the
suffrage was more important than a re-distri-
bution of seats; and that I hoped, if working
men entered upon a new political movement, it
would be for. manhood suffrage.
What I did say, after several speakers had
preceded me, was that there could be no value
in a re-distribution of seats without equality
in the franchise; and that as my main hope
was to see labour representatives enter Parlia-
ment, the experiences in America and Switzer-
land had led me to look with distrust upon
any re-apportionment of representation that
merely divided constituencies into words,
having one member only, and yet, left un-
touched, what, for the want of a better term,
we called the absolute majority system, which,
in the interest of party, invariably led to the
nomination of rieh, safe, and often mediocre
men—who upon a sharp question that sharply
defines opinion, dare neither say yes nor no
for fear of offence, to any shade of prejudice
or thought. I held that the more democratic
constituencies became, the more was this evil
apparent, and the less did special thought or
individuality obtain presence in representative
bodies.
It therefore became a consideration for
working men, if they wished the direct repre-
sentation of their color, if they should uot at

any conference upon this subject support a
scheme of redistribution like that comprised
in Mr. Walter Morrison's Bill of last session,
which to my mind presented a simplified and
comprehensible modification of Mr. Hare's
plan for personal representation far superior
to the arithmetical and geometrical divisions
contemplated by absolute, equal, electoral
districts, which to keep the balance of repre-
sentation true to population, invalued the
periodical rectification of boundaries, and its
conoommitimt evil (known in America as
Jerrymandering), that of fraudulently arrang-
ing constituencies to suit the interests of the
party in office at the time.
I submit this is a very different argument
than your reporter's summary gives as from
me.
In conclusion let me add that, although
never absent from first to last, I failed to
observe the presence of either Messrs. Lucraft,
Coulson, Harry, or Stafford, at the meeting;
and can assure you neither Cremer nor
Stafford took part in the proceedings.
Yours faithfully,
Tiros. MOTTERSIIEAD.

[The report complained of was supplied to
us in manifold by a reporter who was present,
and who generally attends and reports the
proceedings of these meetings for those who
convene them,—En.]

STANDING ARMIES AND THE
WORKING CLASSES.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
Siu,-7---On looking over your edition of
Saturday last I found that Mr. Bruce had
replied to my letter which appeared in your
edition of September 28th. I had. dismissed
the subject from my mind, thinking that Mr.
Bruce did not think it worth replying to, but
I find that I am mistaken.
Mr. Bruce has got the idea that the peace
party want our army disbanding before courts
of arbitration are fully established. He is
very much mistaken. But what we want (at
least what I want) is, that now we have set
the example of settling disputes by arbitration,
we ought to show that we place full confidence
in such tribunals by reducing our army,
instead of keeping it on a war footing, as it is
at present. He can't see the force of my reason-
ing when I say "England is a nation who will
give justice and have justice without having
recourse to standing armies." I will just ask
him if he does not think that England has
both given justice to America and done justice
to herself by the Geneva Arbitration? I have
only "discovered part of the truth" in regard
to the argument on the police force; they are
"employed to prevent ()rime," besides" bring-
ing men to justice." Certainly they are em,
ployed for that purpose, but Mr. Bruce does
not prove that armies are kept to prevent
crime; on the contrary, they tend to inerease
it, both in time of peace and when engaged.
in war. He does not understand me com-
paring armies to bulldogs; in my opinion a
more tit name I could not have found, for they
are fed and trained in time of peace to be able
to fight and slay each other at their master's
bidding in time of war.
Mr. Bruce says I run away from the ques-
tion, "about our army being a necessity." If
he believes in " arbitration," as he says, how
does he make it out that our " army is a
necessity ?" for those who believe in our
"army being a necessity," surely can't expect
us to think they believe in peaceful "arbitra-
tion." But is our " army " really a
" necessity," as Mr. Bruce says. In what
way is it necessary that we should.
train men, and keep them out of the
pocket of the " working classes," simply to
slay each, other when the noble aristocrats,
that rule our country, say the word? Mr.
Bruce is one of those persons who think that
England owes her existence to her army; they
seem to ignore the fact that this land is called
"Christian England," and, as such, she never
ought to have an army, for Christianity and
war can never go hand-in-hand as they seem
to think they can, for there is not, in my
opinion, any such thing as a "justifiable
war.''
Mr. Bruce, in the first part of his letter,
says "he is anxious that war should be
abolished," and to conclude he says "there is
no other, way of preserving peace than by
being fully prepared for war." He wishes
"war to be abolished," but to abolish it we
must, in his opinion, keep our army ready for
war.
Such reasoning as this I can't understand,
and I think Mr. Bruce does, not see his way
clear when he says one thing in the beginning
of his letter, and then contradicts it at the
dose, If the advocates of "standing armies"
have no better reasons than these, we may
begin to hope that the time is not far distant
when the arguments of the "peace party"
will suit the " world as it is."
In conclusion, I may say that if to be
" patriotic," I must support what I think is a
groat evil and ought not to be tolerated, I fear
I shall have to go down
To the vile dust from whence I sprung,
Unwept, unhonourod, and unsung.
Hoping you will excuse me for trespassing
on your space, I am, yours truly.
J. 13, REDPEARN.

Height, Heekmondwike.

articles.title: LA.NDLORD AND TENANT. To the Editor of the BEE•IIIVE.
articles.text:
LA.NDLORD AND TENANT.
To the Editor of the BEE•IIIVE.

Snt,—My object is to set before you the
facts of the case, and with this view will en-
deavour to set the question in a new light.

We are told by everybody that if the land
was properly cultivated, the produce would be
doubled. Why, then, is not this done ? Be-
cause it is not generally thought that farming
is profitable. Suppose you were to say to a
cotton spinner about to start a son in business,
you know cotton spinning is not what it used
to ; try farming; he would say, no.
Now I really believe farming would pay
better than cotton spinning, but, of course,
the pioneers might be ruined, as is the case
with all new trades. If Mr. Meehi were to
sell his farm to-morrow, I do not expect
he would get back his cash outlay, to say
nothing of his time and labour.
Farming in England can as little be carried
on without capital and machinery as cotton
spinning. No doubt a farmer may, and
actually does, squat on the land
.just as an
Irishman, or a negro in the .West Indies;
but this is not cultivating the laud, or bene-
fiting his countrymen.
On the one hand we are told 500 millions
are necessary to the proper cultivation of the
land; on the other we see that 500 millions have
escaped through the waste-pipe of foreign
speculation in American, French, Turkish, and
other loans and shares.

This money, if spent on the soil, would go
entirely in labour, digging drains, levelling
hedges and ditches, erecting machinery—in
all the infinitely numerous details which dis-
tinguish good farming from bad.

One thing depends on another. You cannot
use a steam plough except in largo fields
which are well levelled, and, indeed, the com-
petition of rnachiuely is more with horse than
manual labour—every farm almost might
have water-power.
The farmer constantly repeats these words :
—" It is the labour that beats you." No
doubt labour not assisted by machinery is too
dear oven at the present low rates. The farmer
wants about four times the labour he has got.

The one thing to be kept in sight is how to
get the capitalist to invest this 500 millions in
the cultivation of the land. As things are
now, there are 4,259,795 acres in Ireland that
the Government cannot get any bid. The
capitalist will not take them oven as a gift,
the condition being attached that he shall
reclaim them!

Land, as land, has no value at all, as may
be seen in the colonies, and even here. If you
were to send a contractor down to an average
farm, and ask him to say for what he would
erect a similar farm-house and buildings, and
execute the drainage and other works, he
would name a sum vrhich at 7 per cent. would
come to more than the rent of the farm.

Seven per cent. is, I believe, the usual return
a builder looks to for hi y money, and as 21 por
cent. is all that landed property returns, one
can easily see how this may be.
Supposing the 500 millions were spent in
improving the land, the following results
might be expected
In the first place, more agricultural labour-
ers would be employed at good wages. This
would prevent the constant immigration of
labourers into London, estimated, -Irish in-
eluded, at 80,000 per annutu. Next, meat
would be plentiful at 61 per lb., and the
quartern loaf would not rise above (31., but
generally be sd.
Compare these advantages with any benefit
to be derived from dividing the laud into half-
acre lots. . .

Capital is the mother of wages. Not but
what it would be desirable that such labourers
should have a cottage and garden at perhaps
3s. 6d. per week rent, or 7 per cent. on the
cost of the cottage and land.
It must be borne in mind that cottages
sometimes diminish the value of an estate,
and do not in any case increase it.
This agricultural question is the greatest of
all questions, and is now peculiarly pressing,
because we are, I think, entering on a period
of commercial depression, which must not be
intensified by the French Loan, which is not
only of unprecedented amount, but the instal-
ments are spread over a very long time.
How sad it is that 500 millions, which
might have been spent in wages here' should
have been invested in foreign loans and shares !
—I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
0. W. FIELD.
13, Kildare-gardens.

POST-OFFICE PORTERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-lIIvE.

SIR,—You will be doing a justice to a large
and increasing body of servants belonging to
this class of Post-office officials employal at St.
Afartin's-le-Grand, and at the London district
offices, by inserting in your journal some of
the many grievances of one of the most hard-
done-by and forgotten class of public servants.
1 am sorry even in your excellent paper,
that while the claims of the sorters, letter
carriers, and assistants have been ventilated,
the porters have been somehow overlooked.
Any person not having an acquaintance with
the working of the Post-office might be quite
ignorant of such a class in the service. When
we enter the service we have to undergo the
strictest investigation as tp character, dating
as far back as our first school, as well as a '
medical examination. After all this we have
to commence at a salary of 18s. per week, and
it is three years before we attain to 215., and
and it is not until we have been in the
service seven years that we reach the maxi-
mum of 255. per week. Our hours of duty
cover 17 hours. Most of the men have to
leave their bed at 3 a.m. in order to be on
duty at 4or 430 a.m. Two attendances a
day, and it is 8 p.m. or later before they are
off duty. Many of the men, throng, i the ex-
ceeding low wages they receive, having to live
at a distance from the office, have their rest
broken by rising shortly after midnight in
order to be at their duty at the specified time.
Such a thing as a Saturday half-holiday is
unknown at the Post-office, and a man is dt-
prived of having even a night off duty without
paying for it. As matters stand at present
no chance of promotion is afforded to men be:
longing to the class of porters, although seine
of the most responsible duties of the office are
performed by them ,formerly done 1y sub-sorters,
viz., store ofiioe, bag room, and sorting duties.
I should like to enquire, through the medium
of your paper, what has been done, or whether
any steps are intended to be taken by the
delegates appointed by the porters What
the porters ought to strive for should be to gEt
the barrier broken down_ which exists betwe( n

them and the letter carriers, and to be classi-
fied, at least, under as favourable conditions
as the letter carriers.

By the arrival of the Australian mail we

connection with the so-called labour trade in

went, however, on a "labour cruise" among

set lire to the ship. The captain and crew
thereupon • tired upon them indiscriminately,
and about seventy were killed and wounded.
Killed and wounded were alike thrown over-
board. The captain and the crew have been
committed for trial at Sydney.

first lecture in America on the Will instant, at
