New York, to a large audience, and was very
well received.

A now public elementary school for blys
was opened on Monday by the School Board
for London in the premises lately occupied as•
a middle-class commercial school, 236, Great
College-street, Camden-town. The premises
have been taken temporarily until the new
school buildings for a thousand children are
erected, for which a site has been purahaial,
Nos. 3 and (3, Sussex-terrace, near at land 4

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

]or Majesty the Queen has sent her cus-
tomary donation of three sovereigns to the
wife of a labourer in Woolwich Arsenal, and
to the wife of a workman living at Tunbridge
Wells—both of whom have bore triplets.

In the Albert Assurance Society ease, the
arbitrator ord Cairns) has given warning
that all claims will be barred which are not
sent in before the 30th of November next.

In the small church belonging to the Monas-
tery of St. Augustine, atßamsgate, on Sunday,
an imposing and significant ceremony took
place. This was no less than the oonferring a
mitre on an Abbot, according to the ancient
rite, which resembles in most respects the con-
secration of a Bishop, and indeed has nearly
the same effect. The event is noteworthy OFi
being the first of its kind since the Reforma-
tion.

Father Ignatius, on Sunday night, in the
Brighton Concert Hall, conducted what was
sailed a " Requiem " for the soul of the late
Mr.Turchas, another reoalcitrant against the
known civil requirements of the Church of
England. Although much in it was strained
eltui theatrical, the service, in its personal
part, was earnest and heartfelt.

Mr. John Dorri.ngton, M.A.., Ph.D., F.L.S.,
and G.8.L., of Ripley College Derbyshire, has
been brought up for the lase time. at Marl-
borough-street for obtaining money by false
pretences—that is obtaining charitable con-
tributions for a distressed lady, who was, in
fact, his own sister, and was not in distress at
all, inasmuch as she filled the place of house-
keeper in a family. Ile was imprisoned upon
three charges, but notice was given of appeal.

The Queen of the Netherlands arrived at
Ford Castle, Northumberland, on Monday
evening, on a few days visit to the Dowager
Marchioness of Waterford.

Captain Bedford Pim, it is stated, will contest
Richmond in the Conservative interest.

A vacancy has occurred in the representation
of Orkney and Shetland by the death of Mr.
pandas, who reprepresented that constituency
from 1837 to 1847, and again from 1852 to the
present time. In 1537, and again in 1841, he
was returned without a contest; in 1847 Mr.
Arthur Anderson defeated him by 209 to 183;
in 1852, Mr. Daubs stood again, but the seat
was contested by Mr. John Inglis. Mr.
Dandas was returned by 227 to 194. The last
contest took place in 1868, when Mr. Dundas
beat bis opponent, Mr. Riddell, by 715 to 446.

Ilk Two Roman Catholic Bishops—the Right
Rey. Dr. W. Weathers, coadjutor Bishop of
Westminster, and the Right Rev. Dr. Herbert
Vaughan, Bishop of Salford—were conseorated
at the Roman Catholic Cathedral, Salford, on
Monday.

Another letter from M. Michel Chevalier to
the secretary of the Manchester Chamber of
Commerce relative to the new French Treaty
is published; in which he says :—" The Chief
of the French Government has but one object,
viz., the abolition of the principle of low duties
on imports; and he pursues this objeet, not as
a man guided by reason, but as one possessed
by a dominant purpose; and in this Manner
the interests of I'ranoe are saorificed."

The Council of the Working Men's Inter-
national Peace Association, it is stated, intend
to hold meetings in various provincial towns,
in furtherance of their views and to hold a
conference in Manchester in November.

What is described as "a great mass meeting"
of the inhabitants of Sheffield was held in
Paradise-square in that town on Monday to
protest against the Licensing Act and the
restrictions under it imposed by the borough
magistrates. Resolutions were passed de-
nouncing the Act as an unjust and arbitrary
measure.

A lifeboat service, whereby the crew of the
Zebre, a French ketch, were saved, is reported.
The vessel, which was at anehor of Dynichurch,
parted from her anchor soon after the crew
were taken off, and became a total wreck.

The Ootober sessions of the Central Crimi-
nal Court was opened at the Old Bailey on
Monday morning. The calendar contained
the names of 72 prisoners, of whom two are
for murder, one for attempting to murder,
three for manslaughter, and two for per-
jury.

The inquest on the bodies of the man and
woman who ware recently found dead in the
house No. 18, Golden-square, was resumed on
Monday. No additional evidence was given
as to identification, but it was stated that they
appeared to be.of the middle class of life, and
the medical evidence was dear that they had
died from the effeets of strychnine. The jury
returns* verdict to that effect.•

The death is announced of Sir Alexander
Duff Gordon, the third baronet, Commissioner
of Inland Revenue. Ife was secretary to Sir
Cornewall Lewis when Chancellor of the Ex-
chequer. Ile is succeeded in ths baronetcy
by his son Maurice, who was born in 1849.
The first baronet, Sir James Duff, was British
Consul at Cadiz, and the baronetcy was entailed
upon his nephew, William Gordon, who took
the name of Gordon in addition to his own.

A man named Patrick Smith murdered his
wife in Newcastle on Tuesday afternoon. On.
going home for dinner he found his wife drunk
in bed and no dinner ready. He dragged her
out, and is supposed to have kicked and other-
wise violently assaulted her. He left her
bleeding on the floor, and on the Police enter-
ing the house later in the day the woman was
quite dead. Dr. Hume examined the body,
and stated that she had bled to death. The
police apprehended the prisOner, who has been
charged on suspicion of causing his wife's
death.

At the Newmarket Farmers' Club dinner on
Tuesday night Lord Royston appealed to the
farmers present whether they would rather have
high rents and no game, or low rents and game.
The whole of them, with scarcely an exception,
replied high rents and no game. This answer
rather nonplussed the noble Viscount, who
.added that the question was, as he said before,
one of contract between landlord and' tenant.
He hoped that the landlords generally made
compensation to tenants for injuries done.
The meeting expressed its thorough disapproval
of the preservation of ground game, and in
favour of the tenant farmers being the land-
lords' keepers.

It is authoritatively stated that there is no
truth in the report from Richmond as to the
persons who committed suieide in Golden-
square being Captain and Mrs. Douglas, late of
6, Upper Park-place, Richmond.

The first show of the Oxford Poultry and
Pigeon Show commenced at the Corn Ex-
change and Town Hall, Oxford, on Wednesday
morning, when 800 pens of birds were sub-
mitted for public exhibition. Notwithstanding
the unpleasant rain the show was extensively
patronized. The judges, were Mr. W.• B.
Tegetineier, Mr. if. Jones, and Mr, F.
Esquiland.

A Grand. Requiem High Mass was sung at
the Church of the Jesuits, Farm-street, Berkley.
square, on Wednesday morning, for the repose
of the soul of her Highness the Princess de
Ligne, who died last Friday. The Church was
draped in black, studded with the arms of the
deceased. After the ceremony the remains
were borne to St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery,
Kensal-green.

• The signs of a reduction ia the price of coal
in South-west Lancashire are said to be becom-
ing more apparent day by day. The proximity
of these fields to the port of Liverpool has
caused high prices to be maintained much
longer than would have otherwise been the
case • but the appearanoe on some of the pit
banks, of thousands of tons clearly indicates
that ere long there will be a fall in the price of
coal. Large buyers are somewhat chary of
making fresh contracts, and as the existing ones
expire they simply buy to satisfy their
im-
mediate wants. Although the prices seem to
be maintained at the pits, it is understood that
large consumers buy at some reduction, and
the public generally must of necessity soon
enjoy the same advantages.

The Archbishop of Dublin, in opening the
synods of the united dioceses of Dublin, Glen-
dalough, and Kildare, referred somewhat
discouragingly to the financial position; but,
on the whole, it appeared that their average
income of incumbents will be at least equal to
what it was under the old regime, without
trenching on the capital of the Church's
property.

A young man, 23 years of age, was on
Wednesday convicted at the Mansion House
of having smuggled a large quantity of foreign
manufactured tobacco and cigars. He was
fined £lOO, with the alternative of six months'
imprisonment.

A. cab-driver and proprietor was on Wednes-
day summoned at the Clerkenwell Police-court
for having wilfully impeded a tramway car in
the Kingsiand-road. The defendant drove his
vehicle in front of the car at a walking pace
for more than a quarter of a mile, and when
'remonstrated with by the conductor struck
him a blow with his whip. The magistrate at
first imposed a penalty of £4 and the costs, but
afterwards, on an earnest appeal by the
defendant, and no objection being made by the
prosecution, the fine was reduced by one-lialf.

Mr. John Vale, who is described as a
cf portly old gentleman," was fined 10s. at the
Worship-street Poliee-Court on Monday for
alighting from a train at the Cambridge heath
Station on the Great Eastern Railway, while
the train was in motion, Which caused him to
fall out and roll on the ground.

Mr. Stanley received a rather demonstrative
reception from the mill-girls of Paisley, a few
days ago. Two thousand or them surrounded
the explorer, who was in the end glad to escape
to his Carriage.

A terribly exciting scene occurred on the
Cornwall railway on Tuesday afternoon. The
driver of a mineral train, descending the in-
eline which runs from Brungalon through St.
Austell to Par, lost control over it, in conse-
quence of defective breaks, and the train
dashed at a frightful and increasing speed
down the line up which a mail train was ap-
proaching. The driver of the passenger train
saw the danger when the mineral train was a
mile off, and reversed his engines. The pas-
sengers watched with breathless terror from
every window the descending train. There
was a race for life to Par, but the mail train
was there first by, twenty yards, and all
danger was avoided. The passengers over-
whelmed the brave man with their thanks
and gifts.

Lord Massey's seat, the Hermitage, near
Castle Connell, county Limerick, was burned
to the ground on Monday, and all the valuable
contents destroyed. The loss is estimated at
£15,000, which is only covered by insurance
to a small extent.

The ScotBman understands that the Bishop
of Natal intends, at an early date, to publish
the results of his researches on the Pentateuch
In the form of lectures, written in a popular
style, the six volumes on the subject he has
already published being found too bulky and
erudite for general readers.

A Californian telegram has just been re-
ceived at Southampton stating that a vessel
hailing from that port has been taken up at
San Francisco to carry wheat to Europe, at a
freightage of £5 per ton. California has
200,000 tons of wheat to spare this year, and
150,000 tons are already on their way to
various parts of the world.

Mr. Dixon, M.P., presiding at Birmingham
on Tuesday night, at the second lecture of the
series, under the auspices of the Nonconfor-
mist Committee, denied that Dissenters, in
moving for disestablishment, were actuated by
jealousy of the Church. He believed that the
people of the country might fairly be divided
into those who attended Church services, those
who went to -other oommunione' and those who
attended no place of worship. These divisions
would not be very unequal, and that being so,
there was no basis for the charge of jealousy.

The ceremony of rooting the evicted tenants
of Captain Nolan in the soil took place on
Monday in the ROD3RI2 Catholic Chapel at
Cummer, a few miles from Tuam, county Gal-
way. The Archbishop of Tuam did not attend,
and the other neighbouring Bishops sent letters
of apology. The Bishop of Clonmel arrived
at the end of the proceedings. The unfavour-
able weather prevented any open-air'demon-
stration.

At a meeting of ratepayers of St. Pancras,
on Tuesday evening, the following resolution
was adopted :--" That, in the opinion of this
meeting, the School Board for London has lost
the confidence of the ratepayers of this parish
by a course of extravagant expenditure in
creating schools, which may have the effect
of closing the schools hitherto supported by
voluntary contributions, and more particularly
in purchasing a site for £lB,OOO for the erec-
tion. of offices on the Thames Embankment, at
an enormous cost to the ratepayers.' This
resolution, nearly identical with those already
adopted, was ordered to be forwarded to the
Privy Council on Education and the School
Board.

The text of the award given by the Emperor
of Germany in the San .Tuan Boundary arbi-
tration states that His Majesty, having taken
into consideration the statements of the ex-
perts and jurists appointed by him to report
upon the contents of the Cases and Counter
Cases, has decided that the boundary through
the Haro Channel is most in accordance with
the true interpretation of the Treaty of 1846.

In the Spanish Congress, Senor Garrido de-
clared the other day that the Radical party
only existed by the tolerance of the Rep!ibli-
cans, and Senor Figments expressed the opinion
that the present Ministry would be the last
under King Amadeo. Senor Zorilla, however,
said that he and his colleagues were not
frightened by this declaration of war; and
the Bill under discussion calling out 40,000
men, which the Republicans opposed, was
passed by 507 to 54 votes.

Writing to an American correspondent,
Earl Russell declares his wish to see the
material wants of Ireland fairly examined, the
necessary remedies fairly tried, and means
employed to bring about the improvement and
prosperity of the country, But his lordship
most earnestly deprecates the setting up of
an Irish Parliament, which would lead, to the
waste of all Ireland's energies in political con.
tention,

2, 1872;

Last week the total number of paup3r3 in
the metropolitaudistricts 171,3 103,203, of whom
33,763 were in workhouses and 09,445 reoeiv ed
out-door relief. Compared with the years
1871,1870, ~and 1869`raspsotively, these fig.ures
show a decrease of 12,266, 27,992, and 30,4 03.
The number of vagrants reeieved on the last
day of the week was 842.

A superannuated policeman, named William.
Crocker, who was recently committed to prison
from the Clerkenwell Police-court, in default
of obtaining sureties to keep the peace towards
his wife, strangled himself on Wednesday
morning in the House of Detention.

•
At a spontaneous meeting of influential in-
habitants of Leamington, held on Wednesday
night at the Town-hall, the chairman of the
Local Board was directed to request the
favour of our insertion of an. authoritative
denial of the alleged existence of typhus fever
in that town or neighbourhood; and arrange-
ments were made for holding a public meet-
ing on Alonday to detnonstra,to by statistic
the high sanitary state of the town.

A London merchant has offered a munificent
contribution ia aid of the extension of the
foreign missions of the Church in the form of a
subscription of £l,OOO per annum for five
years to the Society for the Propagation of the
Gospel in Foreign Parts.

It is propable that further legal changes
will be made during Michaelmas Term. Loid
Penzance, who was appointed Judge-Ordinary
of the Divorce Court in the autumn of 1863,
in succession to the late Sir C. Cresswell, has
found it necessary- to send in his resignation
hi cOnsequence of ill-health. Baron Martin,
who has been a puisne judge in the Court of
Exchequer 22 years, and is now 72 years of
age, is mentioned as being likely to take the
place of Lord'Penzence.

Another ease of a missing man is reported.
At the Lambeth Pollee-court on Monday Mrs.
Elizabeth Stone the wife of a butcher in
Brandon-street, 'Walworth-road, stated that
her husband left home on Thursday morning
to go to the Metropolitan Meat Market, and
was to return to breakfast, but ,he had not
Educe been heard of.

Aceording to a Roman paper, the rope,
whenreeently asked by Cardinal Cullen to take
some steps on behalf of the Galway priests, ,-
refused to do so, and !poke with regret Of the ..
disobedience of Irish olergy.

A telegram from a correspondent at Nice ,
announces that the train from Marseilles to. -
that city ran off the rails on Saturday, and
that a Scotch lady died from the shook.

A reciprocal declaration has been signed at
Berne on behalf of the British Government and
the Canton Vaud, regulative of the principles
on which legacy or suceession duties shall be
evied on the property of citizens of either
country dying in the other. Its purport as
affecting British. subjects is, that unless they
have formally applied to be domiciled in ,
the canton, only property real or personal
whioh they actually possess there shall become ,
subject to the above duties.

The usual collections in aid of the charitable
institutions of Birmingham were made on
Sunday in the various churches and chapels
of the town. The total collected was
£3,057 3s. Bd.

Mr. Hope Scott, whose recent illness in.
Edinburgh caused some anxiety to his friends,
is again in a critical condition. His children,
who have been residing at Abbotsford, were on
Saturday telegraphed for to proceed to London,
where he now lies. He is suffering from fatty
degeneration of the heart, and is b3ing st
tended by Sir William Gull, in addition to his
own medical attendant.

-
Cardinal Cullen's journey to the Vatican,
according to a Roman journal, was undertalcon
in the view of urging the f'ope to interfere
on behalf of the persecuted " Roraan
Catholic clergy of Galway; but the mission
has altogether failed, the Holy Father strongly
condemning the behaviour of the Irish clergy,
who "only obeyed his instructions when they
could turn them to good account, but willingly
disobeyed them when °ailed upon to sacrifice
their
,palsions to the commands of his Holi-
ness,'

:It is said confidently that M. Thiers dis-
courages all propositions which are made for
conferring upon him the Presidency of the
Republic for life. Those who are most inti-
mate with him affi.rra positively that he would.
prefer to be chosen President for four yearsr
with a right of re-election. -

A large number of fish-merehatits, sales-
men, and others interested in the trade, met
at Lowestoft, on Tuesday night, and resolved
to send a deputation to the Foreign Moe to
represent the injurious effects upon British
commeroe of the terms of the new French,
Treaty hilts referpnce to fish imports.

Nov. 2, 1872

According to an official statement published
in Washington, the public debt of the United
States has been paid off at the rate of one
hundred million dollars a year for the last
three years.

The Dowager Marchioness of Queensberry
has written a friendly letter to Mrs. Kelly,
wife of Robert Kelly, who was tried for the
murder of Talbot, and subsequently sentenced
to 15 years' penal servitude for shooting one
of the policemen who arrested him. The mar-
chioness condoles with Mrs. Kelley, encloses
her a sum of money, and promises to under -
take the education of her eldest son. Up to a
few weeks since—when he left for America—
the son of Larkin, one of the men executed at
Manchester for the murder of Sergeant Brett,
was being educated at a leading Dublin school,
at the marchioness's expense.

The direotors of the Iron and Citizen Steam-
boat Company have announced that they in-
tend to make a reduction in their fares.

The Rev. Dr. Marshall, a prominent United
Presbyterian Minister, who has taken a lead-
ing part in ecolehiastical and educational con-
troversies in Scotland, has been presented with
£l,OOO as a testimonial.

The Great Eastern Railway Company, have
offered to grant season tickets for half the
usual. rice to all post-office employes living
on their lines, provided that the Company are
exempted from all passenger claims from such
employes for unpunctuality or accidents.

M. Renan has received from the Liberals at
Rome the warmest welcome, and from the
clerical journals almost unmeasured abuse. In
a semi-private speech, on the occasion of a
banquet to his honour, the author of the "Vie
de Jesus" declared that he had no confidence
in the definitive establishment of a Republic,
notwithstanding all the ability of M. niers to
attempt to restore the Temporal Power.

Though final results are not yet known, it
seems beyond doubt that the majority of the
National Councillors elected in Switzerland on
Sunday are pro-Revisionists.
---
Mr. Stanley visited Ayr, the Land of Burns,
on Tuesday, and partook of a thoroughly na-
tional repast in the cottage in which the poet
was born.

A Home Rule meeting was held in the
Ulster Hall, Belfast, on Tuesday night, and
was very largely attended. Mr. G. Bigger,
the Home Rule candidate for Londonderry,
presided, and Mr. Smyth, M.P., was one of the
speakers. Resolutions were adopted, declaring
that " while the meeting claimed for the Irish
people the right
,to make laws to rule them-
selves, they indignantly repudiated the asser-
tion that they wished to destroy the integrity
of the British Empire and promote the ascen-
dancy of any religious party."

Several valuable seams of coal have been
discoverei in South Chili' and numerous com-
panies have been formed for working them.

Lord Boyne (Baron Branoepoth of the United
Kingdom) expired on Tuesday, at his residence
Branoepeth Castle, near Durham, the imme.
diate cause of death being an attack of gout.
The deceased nobleman, was in his 76th year.

The National Society for Promoting the
Education of the Poor in the Principles of the
Established Church have received from a City
merchant the intimation of his intention to
contribute the Munificent sum of £2,000 in
aid of the funds. Of the, society at the present
educational crisis.

The first of this year's autumnal series of
lectures to young men was given on Tuesday in
St. Paul's Cathedral. The Rev. Canon Gregory
delivered an address on the Bonds of Society,
Past and Present, and this is to be followed by
two others from him on the same topic. About
1,000 persons, consisting solely of men were
present. The service was very short, and with
the lecture, occupied only an hour and a
quarter.

The Rev. Dr. Halley was on Tuesday pre-
sented with a testimonial as on indication of
the esteem and affection in which he is held
by the ministers. and members of the Congre-
gational body.

The working of the Licensing Act has been
reported on favourably by the Chief Constable
of Birmingham, in which town, during the
past two months there has been a decrease of
crimes connected with drunkenness to the
extent of 20 per cent.

in receiving a deputation of his constituent,
on Tuesday on the subject of the income-taxs
the Attorney-General expressed his wish for
the abolition of the impost, but he declined to
pledge himself to vote for its extinction. As
long as the national expenditure remained at
its present figure he law no hope of getting
rid of the tax, for he did not see where the six
millions now raised by it were to come from.

Terrible accounts are sent from the United
States as to the ravages of the epidemic among
horses, which has now spread from Canada to
the seaboard cities of the Union. In New
York alone it is stated that 30,000 animals
are sick; and, though comparatively few
deaths have occurred, the inconvenience to
traffic is very great, ocean-bound steamers
even being unable to complete their cargoes
for want of haulage.

Mr. Blake, leader of the Government in
Ontario, has resigned, his place being taken
by Vice-Chancellor Mowatt.

The Hon. Miss Grosvenor, one of the guests
invited to Knowsley Hall, Lord Derby's seat
in Lancashire, during the visit of the Queen
of Holland, left her jewellery in her dressing-
room at eight in the evening; and on return-
ing at eleven she found that the room had been
entered, and all her valuables taken away.
Apart from their intrinsic worth, something
like £3,000, the jewels were highly prized by
the owner for their personal associations.
The robber or robbers seem to have got clear
away.

It was announced on Tnesday that Mr. T.
Hughes, M.P., will not come forward at the
next election as a candidate for Frome. Mr.
Donald Nicoll (Liberal) a former member,
and Mr. H. Lopes and Lord Edward Thynne,
M.P., (Conservatives) are probable candidates

Messrs. Brighty and Weston attended at a
meeting held in the Gladstone Hall, at Lei-
cester, on Tuesday evening, as a deputation of
the Anti-Game-Law League. Resolutions
were adopted, denouncing in very strong terms
the effects of the game laws.

"International Arbitration and Woman's
Place in it" was the subject of a paper read
at Manchester on Tuesday night, by Mrs.
King, of London, in the Free Trade Hall, to
a large audience, who passed a resolution
favouring the formation of a women's peace
society, with a view to promote the settlement
of international disputes on the principles of
reason and justice.

Bad news continues to come from the north-
east of Europe. Rinderpest, as well as cholera,
has broken out at Warsaw, with destructive
effect; and cholera has crossed the German
and Austrian frontiers—eases being reported
from Dantzie, Kuhn, and Buda.

Differences between the German and Chinese
Governments in regard to the recent Commer-
cial Treaty have led to new negotiations—but
not, as has been affirmed, to a break-up of the
agreement.

In responding for the Navy, at Reading, on
Tuesday, Mr. Shaw-Lefevre assured his con-
stituents that the Admiralty were fully im-
pressed with the supreme necessity of not
allowing our iron-elad.s to lag behind those of
any other country.

We understand that Messrs. John Brogden
and Sons, railway contractors to the New
Zealand Government, have a scheme of
colonization in process of arrangement with
the Government of New Zealand, by which
the workmen, who are on their landing placed
at railway or navvy work, may be taken off
as the work progresses and put to cultivate
plots of land or farms of their own, the free-
hold of which will be handed over to them
on terms of easy, repayment, similar to the
arrangement under which they are now
forwarded as working emigrants to that coun-
try.

At Marlborough-street a painful exposure
was made of the Sunday evening amusements
peculiar to the hobbedehoys of New-street,
Bond-street. Some thirty or forty lads and
girls, in a kind of organized disorder, rushed
about the street, hustling decent passengers,
and committing the grossest outrages on un-
protected female wayfarers. Mr. Newton had
to deal with three of the gang, two of whom
--girls—he fined 10s. each, making the other
prisoner, a young man, enter into recognisance
to keep the peace for thrce mouths.

A lady named Plenty, the wife of an engi-
neer at Newbury, committed suicide on Satur-
day morning at Brighton, by leaping into the
sea. She had been suffering from ill-health
and lowness of spirits.

At Ramsgate, on Tuesday, Earl Granville
distributed the prizes and certificates to the
successful candidates at the recent Oxford
local exantinations.

---
A Volunteer "of no occupation" who bad
injured wiih his ride an unfortunite woman
in a quarrel early on Sunday morning in the
neighbourhood of Saddler'sVells, has been
fined £3 by the magistrate at Cierkenwell
Police-court.

The Devastation steamed out of Portsmouth
harbour on Tuesday morning, when the
second contractors' trial of her engines was
made, and pronounced satisfact)ry.

In the case of the young woman who lately
died in Woodohester-street, from an attack of
typhoid fever, after travelling from Leaming-
ton the jury have found that death was the
result of natural causes, and expressed their
opinion that sufficient judgment had not been
shown in the removal of the deceased, and
that there was ample evidence of the water-
supply of Leamington being in an unsatisfac-
tory state.

It is stated that Mr. Samuel Laing will offer
himself as a candidate for the representation
of Orkney and Shetland, vacant by the death
of Mr. Dundas.

The Lords of the Admiralty in celebration
of their recent visit to Chatham Dockyard,
having ordered that all the men employed in the
yard should have a half-holiday to• day (Satur-
day), the men have been working overtime
to make up the time for the remainder of the
day, so as to have a whole holiday on that
day.

The Bradford Chamber of Commerce have
decided to support the proposal of Sir Sydney
Waterlow to establish a Central Chamber and
Tribunal of Commerce in London.

It is said that Mr. Darwin is in feeble
health, and will, therefore, be unable to be put
in nomination for the Reotorship of Aberdeen
University.

The sea-going qualities of the new ironelad,
Devastation, underwent a severe trial in the
gale off Spithead, on Wednesday, during
which she stood out to sea and weathered the
storm with, it is said, "absolute immobility."
All night long, and all day too, the Devasta-
tion rode out the gale at Spithead with only
the one Martin anehor she dropped after her
trial trip to bring her up at her station.

At the annual meeting of the Bristol School
of Art, on Wednesday, it was reported that
the subscriptions amounted to only £35. The
Mayor (Mr. Proctor Baker) and several of
the citizens complained of the want of sym-
pathy for art among the upper classes in
Clifton and Bristol.

At Messrs. Debenbam, Storr, and Sons'
auction, on Wednesday, 3,000 carats of dia-
monds from South Africa, received by the last
two mails, were disposed of in about fifty lots.
The highest price obtained was for lot 652,
which found a buyer at ten guineas per carat.
The sale amounted to about £13,670.

French news from Rome is to the purport
that the Versailles Government will not inter-
fere, even to the extent of offering advice, in
the discussions of the bill with regard to reli-
gious corporations—a quite gratuitous intima-
tion, it should seem; that M. Thiers has in-
formed the Princess Clotilde of her freedom
to live in France if she chooses; and that
next month negotiations for a Franco-Italian
Treaty of Commerce will begin.

M. Crftaieux was elected President, and Sir
F. Goldsmid, M. Gompertz (Vienna), and M.
Lazarus (Berlin),Vice-Presidents of the Jewish
Conference at Brussels yesterday. The object
of the gathering is to obtain, if possible, by
international intervention, some change for the
better in the condition of the Jews in Rou-
mania, which has been for so many years a
scandal to Europe.

The owners of the Atrato have decided to
abide by the decision of the Government
officials as to whether she is fit to proceed on
her voyage to Melbourne. Meanwhile, the
vessel has been sent into dock at Keyham to
receive new
_main shafts. The first-class
passengers are lodged in the hotels at the
owner's expense, and if they prefer it will have
repaid to theta half the passage-money.
Weather, rain incessant; wind, W.S.W., half

M. Thiers has been definitively assured by
Count Arnim that the occupied departments
shall be evacuated by the 4th of November.
General Dacrot has addressed to the troops
under his command an order of the day, in
which he says: "More impenous, more sacred
duties were never imposed on the army to be-
come educated, disciplined, and strong." He
hopes it may not be necessary to use painful
severity towards enemies at home, but hints
the Germans may one day regret " having
rent their hearts and torn from their mangletl
hands the dearest children of France."

Council, on -Wednesday, Alderman Watkin
took the Mayor to task for being present at
the luncheon at Salford, when the Roman
Catholic bishops were consecrated, and at
which the health of the Pope preceded that of
the goeen. The Mayor replied, that he ac-
cepted th:- invtation to the luncheon without
hesitation, nod would do the same again if
asked.

from all causes in these towns was at the rate

estimated to be living. In the metropolis,

the former having been 115 and the latter 101
below the average. London is just now re-

TESTIMONIAL
TO
MR. ALEXANDER 2/VDONALD,

President of Miners' National Association, and

Miners' Parliamentary Deputation.
FOR-more than a Quarter of a Century
eighteen years incessantly has Mr.
M,Donald laboured to get the Miners of the
United Kingdom more protection to their lives in
following their hazardous occupation --a shorter
hours of labour and education for the young—just
contracts of services; in short to enumerate all
the provisions would be out of place here—they
are, besides, so well-known to all that they do not
need to be mentioned.

Suffice it to say that nearly every one of tho
provisions he has so long claimed as the Miners'
right have now been incorporated in the Mines
Act of 1872, and already have groat changes been
effected in the condition of the mining population
through his labours, but these will be still greater
when the new Act comes into operation.

It is not too much to say that in the long years
of toil, almost without hope, Mr. M‘Donald has
made many sacrifices to health and comfort that
he might have otherwise obtained. At the con-
clusion of the werk so great, we deem this a fit
and proper time to tender to him some substantial
recognition of his many services to the cause of
the Miner, and in general to the cause of human
progress. To the Miners we would say show
your gratitude by your works in aid of the
Testimonial—let it be worthy of the man. To
others we say help.
I am, yours respectfully,
THOMAS WILSON Chairman,
Mid and East Lothian.

OUR POOR AGITATORS.

A. REFORMER of last century, who suffered
prosecution and. imprisonment for promul-
gating his opinion, when on his trial called.
himself 41 the unfeed advocate of the disin-
herited seed of ADAM." In plain language,
he was what was then and what la now very
much dreaded and hated, namely an " agita-
tor." It is the fashion at present for every
man to gird at the" agitator." Every stupid
member of Parliament; every lawyer, who
has grown rich by selling his tongue to the
highest bidder; every minister of the Church,
who has by any means crawled. into a
bishopric; every man of any kind, who is
rich or who expects to be so, however
his money may come, being eatisited

with things as they are, and with him-
self, and quite prepared to bear patiently
the sufferings of others, is angry with
the troublesome agitator, whose delight
it is to excite discontent and foster a spirit of
change. It would be tedious to enumerate
those, who, within the. last few months, have
been howling anathemas at the "agitator."
There are many reasons it would appear why
this dangerous person should be discouraged.
All his motives are bad if those who denounce
him are to be believed. He is mercenary,
and only talks for what he gets, though none
of his accusers makes any guess at his income
or the source from when it is derived. He
loves mischief for mischief's sake, and only
interferes that he may set people together by
the ears. And yet when we come to examine
into the matter, we find no case where an
agitator made money by his work, though. we
could mention many cases in which such per-
sous paid rather heavily in purse and person
as a punishment for the performance
of their self-imposed duties. The " agitator"
may, we admit, be unsympathising and sordid;
—may be as bad or worse in many oases than
he is said to be. But, nevertheless, we are
prepared to say that if the lives of all well-
known agitators were written, they would, as
a rule, stand in the very front rank amongst
those who have done most to benefit the huinan
race. Certainly in England we owe much to
our illustrious "agitators." We could point
to many noble proofs of this amongst our great
commonwealth's men, Jorix MILTON being one
of the number. In our own day we have had
some excellent samples. Old WILLIAM COB-
BETT and DANIEL O'CONNELL, though differing
as widely as possible in personal cha-
racter, did each of them right good work for
the people they sought to serve. COBBETT, full
of inconsistencies and prejudices, was one of
the sturdiest and most trenchant of champions
when he attacked an abuse :
A labourer's son, mid squires and lords,
Strong on his own stout legs he stood;
Well-armed in bold and trimehant wit ;
And ~vell they learned that tempted it,
That his was English blood.

O'CONNELL, with all the fire and eloquence
of his land, whatever his mistakes, was still
a true knight in the cause of human liberty,
and it is to him we here in England owe our
triumph over that worst and most accursed
form of tyranny, which imposes penalties on
those who seek to worship Goy in sincerity and
truth. And whatever may be said to his dis-
paragement as a paid "agitator,'' it is certain

that if he had become a paid champ ion of the
wrong ho opposed, his payment might
have been tenfold what it was. Then,
again, what does this nation not owe
to RICIIA.RD COBDEN and JOHN BRIGHT—
both agitators of a most suooessful kind ? They
during their struggles, were abused and hooted
at, they were denounced as " agitators " by

the same sort of knavish and slavish creatures
whose voices are now busy with the same
chorus against those who arc insisting on
bettor conditions of lifo for the agricultural
labourer. These men put broad into the
mouths of millions whom the landlords and
their friends were starving for the promotion
of their fancied interests, and even now the
nation is scarcely conscious of the magnitude
of the boon it has received from the hands of
these men; whilst the
.tongues of those who
abused them are still hot with hissing at the
sound of their names.

The dangerous men in England are
not our "agitators ; " our dangerous classes
are our paupers and thieves, and next
to those the miserable opposers of salu-
tary change which would out our suffering
poor off from all chance of escape from their
misery except through violence and bloodshed.
What a history we should have had in the last
fifty years if the scoffers at agitators had been
strong enough to put them down ! What a
miserable contention of classes! what con-
spiracies,riots, and revolts! what imprisonings,
shootings, and hangings! Friends of property
and order would have given us this; agitators
have saved us from it. Let us be thankful, there-
fore, to the "agitators," and always suspicious
of those who hoot at them anti oppose change,
because their own platters are heaped;
because they suck contentedly at the conduits
qf the State ; because they arc selfish, rtufeel-

ing, unpatriotic, and faithful only to the
nation as a bountiful nursing mother, We do
not include here that crowd of indifferent
people who follow the lead of such persons not
knowing why they do so; we simply mean
tipse flingers of dirt, those abusers of " agi-
tators " who hate the men by whose vigilance
and activity they are rendered insecure in the
enjoyment of degrading prejudices and dis-
honest gains.

PEACEFUL PROSPECTS IN SOUTH
WALES.

TuE iron masters of South Wales have
thought thrice before answering the appeal of
their hands for higher wages by a general
lock-out; and. the third time of thinking
appears to have brought them to their right
minds. The notices issued on the first of
October were withdrawn before the month
had expired. The men have met this step
backwards of the masters in the same spirit.
They too, on their part, have retreated from
the point of strike, and are ready to fall
back upon arbitration. Here, it is expected,
the masters will meet them, not in a hostile
but in a conciliatory attitude; and the result
will be, the constitution of a court of arbitra-
tion, by which it may be hoped that the
question in dispute will be fairly, satis-
factorily, and even amicably settled.
The general public have an interest in these
proceedings between masters and men in the
iron and coal districts over and. above that
which belongs to all the relations of employer
and employed in matters of trade. The price
og coal for all purposes is become a ruling
consideration. A " crisis " in the house-coal
trade of Glamorganshire is declared to be im-
pending. The colliers wanted an advance of
fourpence a ton on the then existing price
charged to dealers and consumers; but the
owners have been able to lay before them
facts and circumstances which induced them
to lower their application by one-half. But,
in the face of a "falling market," even this
concession, it seems to have been felt, could
not be made. The masters, however, offered
to submit the question to arbitration, an offer
which the men, by their delegates, refused.
Before condemning them it is necessary to
know fully and accurately the fads; but it
is always a matter for regret when either
masters or men, but especially the latter, de-
cline that which must be the best way of set-
tling disputes. The notice of strike given on
the first of October expired on Thursday, and if
a strike takes place the labours of six thou-
sand men and boys will be suspended. In a
falling market, too, they will have the worst
of it.

Meanwhile, "stagnation" is the word used in
Staffordshire also to describe the state of the
iron and coal trades. Orders are nearly
executed, and the iron-masters talk of reduc-
ing wages, and of a revision of the arrange-
ments of the Board of Conciliation at Christ-
mas. "If the men claim short weight," it is
urged, "they must accept a reduction of one-
fourteenth in wages." Hero is a matter which
touches the whole iron districts. At the same
time-the South Staffordshire and East Wor-
cestershire coal-owners find themselves in a
condition to cease the look-out, which, in fact,
came to an end on Thursday. Not only have
they plenty of applications from engine..
winders and engineers, but the demand for
coal has fallen off to such an extent that
night-work is to be suspended. The effect of
these circumstances is shown in the Stafford-
shire colliers being more ready than those of
Olamorganshire to come to terms with their
employers. The proposal to refer matters to
arbitration is made by the men, who declare
I themselves willing to abide by the award.

THE CHURCH REALLY IN DANGER.
ACCORDING to the announcements made in
the Conservative papers, we are to have a move
by that party at all future elections which
seems to be regarded by those who announce it
as a sudden stroke of policy before which the
enemies of the "Constitution," and all other
good Tory superstitions must give way. it
would appear that the members of the Devon-
shire Church Institution have, in the case of
the Tiverton Election, decided to make sound-
ness of idea in regard to the Church a testing
cinestion. The friends of the Established

9

Church in Devonshire and elsewhere will no
longer stand idly by whilst Mr. MILL and his
Liberationists are bullying candidates into
declarations of hostility towards the Establish-
ment.

There is, after all, no great harm in

this. Members of Church Institutes, as a
rule, do not vote for candidates opposed to the
Church; generally speaking, they belong to
that section of our politicians called Tories.
Any attitude they may decide to take up,
therefore, will leave things pretty much as
they arc, so far as our Parliamentary candi-
dates are concerned. It may be added, never-
theless, that it will alter things very much so
far as the safety of the Church goes. Hitherto
the opposition to the Church Establishment
has been confined to the various bodies of
Dissenters in the kingdom. Multitudes of
Liberal politicians accept the creed of the
Church as preferable to that of any other, and
with the creed take everything else belonging
to it without caring to question them, or to
make any row about what, upon the whole,
they do not disapprove of. They give a pas-
sive rather than an active assent to things as

they are, and jog on leaving the pioneer-
work of disestablishment to the Dissenters,
who are naturally active enough in such a
work without caring a great deal as to the
political aspect of the question.

There are also large numbers of men per-
_ _

featly indifferent to this question, who would
not enquire at election-time, if a candidate
generally suited their views, whether ho wont

in for disestablishment or not, inasmuch as
they, as a rule, have regarded it as a question
belonging to the future rather than to the
present. They take it for granted that the Estab-
lished Church will last their time, and therefore

they shrug their shoulders and pass on. Now, if
the Conservatives and Church Institute people
make it a test question, as we are informed
they will, the whole complexion of the matter
will be altered. It will become at once a
question of the present, and every active
politician will have to take side, either for
or against it. The man singled out by these
fanatical people as the champion of the
Church will necessarily kayo so many accom-
panying Conservative qualities in him, that
Liberal mon will be bound to give him their
opposition. As, to be announced as the
favourer of a Church Establishment, and at
the same time a nominee or proteg4 of the Con-
servatives, will inevitably place a candidate
full front in antagonism to Liberal progress ;
and in driving such a person out of the field,
the Established Church, defeated in its
champions, could not continue to exist in itself.
By all means, then, let the Conservatives
take the Church under their wing, and make
its disestablishment a test question. They
have taken many things under their protec-
tion before now. They took the Test and
Corporation Acts under their guardianship;
the penal laws against Roman Catholics; the
" Constitution" as it was, with its rotten
borough .ornaments ; the Corn Laws, and
many other very important parts of the
nation's past life. Where are these now?
Gone in the past. And now, according to
their own confession, as a political party they
are already re-adjusting their lines so as to
make them " conterminous " with those of the
attacking enemy. Never was a political party
so befogged. Say what they may, they have
no policy but such as their political enemies
dictate to them. They are always adapting
their lines to those of the attacking foe ; and
what they are, as a party, to-day or to-morrow,
depends altogether on the attitude taken up
by the Liberals. Our Conservatives are in
the habit of being beaten—are used to giving
way; and if their safety, as a party, required
the sacrifice of the Church, they would make
it; wipe their mouths and come up again with
new lines of defence, and talk all the old non-
sense over again about spoliation and destruc-
tion, and Heaven knows what besides. They
aro without a thought to sustain them, or a
man to lead them, and their help, therefore,
on any question, is a danger rather than a
protection.

THE SAN JUAN AWARD AND THE

STA N.DA RD.

THE Standard, we presume, is a fair repre-
sentative of, Conservative lacing °nos. If W 4

io

require to know what the condition of thought
is on the general run of public questions
amongst those who call themselves Conserva-
tives, the truest indication should, we presume,
be sought in the columns of the Standard.
There is a kind of juvenile jauntiness in the
Globe unbecoming Conservative years of dis-
cretion; it is brisk but not solid—pert rather
than intelligent; whilst the older and most
popular organ, true to the old instincts of its
party, is stupidly trucoulent in the belief that
abuse, as it is the oldest, is the most efficient
instrument it can employ for the purpose of
serving the Conservative cause.

Its article on the San Juan Award is a
curiosity in its way. It cannot understand
the new-fangled idea of arbitration, and talks
of cowardice and economy, and bragg,adocia
and. bullying, as if arbitration was, only sub-
mitted to because we are .afraid to fight, and
as if submission to an award given by a
tribunal, in the appointment of which we had
our fair influence, was simply the result of
our being afraid to take up arms in defence of
our honour, and to take upon us the cost of
a war. People of ordinary intelligence could
never look on the matter in this light; nor
could anyone not soaked to the centre in the
stupidest spirit of partizanship, ever think of
giving a Whig or Tory complexion to such a
matter. The two questions in dispute between
us and America were not party questions. We
had the choice of fighting about them, or of
settling them without fighting—and, sensibly
enough, our Government chose the latter
course. We agreed that the most impartial
tribunal possible should be chosen mutually,
and the best, we presume, in the power of both
parties, was done to secure this end. We are
not aware that in setting up the tribunals which
have decided in these cases, one party had the
least advantage over the other. If there was
any reason to suspect foul play a protest should
have been made in time, and the matters in
dispute should have been withdrawn. This
was not done, no protest was.made, no foul
play was alleged. Up to this point we were
thoroughly competent to deal with the matters
in dispute, and to fight about them, whatever
the cost, if We thought proper.

Our Government seems to have had more
faith in the justice of ,:our side than the
Standard, or it might have fought rather than
arbitrated. It is true the award has not
justified this confidence, but we oannot help
that. We might have been wicked enough to
make war the only mode of settlement, or we
may be base enough to go to war even yet,
rather than conform, This it would appear
is what the Standard desires, 13ut what then?
The Standard can find bluster, but could it
secure victory? And even if it could, it would
it be impossible for it to secure us the retention
of our honourable name as a nation? Does it
follow that England cannot find an interns,-

tional tribunal that will do her justice? This

surely cannot be the case, and if not we must
look for our gain in peace and justice over a
number of decisions, and we must take care
that when we make appeals our demands shall
be such as will bring us favourable deci-
sions.

We know our Tory friends are very valiant
and can fight. They struck certain very heavy
blows at the first BONAPiRTt in the interest of
Divine right, at an expense not satisfactorily
met yet, and they afterwards. licked the dirty
boots of his nephew, in defiance of all right,
divine and human. If we arbitrate a case we
have a fair chance of a verdict, if our cause be
a good one. Right has something to do in the
matter, and if we keep ourselves thoroughly
in the right we have nothing to fear. In war
right has nothing to do with the decision;
might alone rules there, and it is quite
possible that the god of battles, who is not
under the control of Shoe-lane, might give a
very damaging verdict against us, in such a
sanguinary and costly suit. It may answer
the interest of our respectable contemporary to
have bulletins of battles three or four times a
week as aids to circulation, or to have an un-
principled hireling or two, like the late" Man-
hattan," to spread the rabies of national hatred.
But however the paper might gain by this, the
nation could only lese. So that on the score of
honour as well as interest, We arc better as
challenged a fight in
things are, than if we

the spirit of the Standard. We do not forget
nor does the nation forget the vile part played
by the Standard in making our Alabama diffi-
oulty, and if j ustice were done to the British tax-
payers,the proprietors of that stupidly scurrilous
print should be compelled to pay handsomel:,
for the disgrace and loss it laboured so in-
dustriously and effectively to bring on the
nation in that unhappy affair.

articles.title: INDICATIONS IN FRANCE.
articles.text:
INDICATIONS IN FRANCE.

THE seven vacant seats in the National
Assembly of France have been filled by fresh
elections, which are acepted as sure indications,
so far, of the set of public opinion. As to the
precise shade of political view characterising
the individual men, there seems room, even
in France, for difference of estimate; much,
more, therefore, among ourselves, who are too
little informed to make these nice distinctions.
But the general result is, beyond doubt,
favourable to Republican sentiment, whether
Conservative or Radical ; unfavourable to
dynastic pretensions or a monarchist restora-
tion under any form.
In one only of the seven departments which
were scenes of contest was the Republican
party unsuccessful. In Morhiban, where the
priests are notoriously intolerant, the people
very bigoted, and the old dogma of Divine
right in Church and State still surviving, the
priests and the proprietors won the day, but
at such a cost of every kind as makes defeat
almost as good as victory to the opposite party
who made it such hard work for them. Per-
haps, indeed, the circumstances of this One
Legitimist triumph afford as strong a proof of
the progress of political thought in France.
8 witzorlaud-wards, as any or even all of the
six Republican victories put together.
M. BEAUVAIS, the losing candidate, who had
but eighteen thousand votes in 1871, against
the thirty - two thousand by which M.
GOIIVILLE, the Legitimist, was then re-
turned, obtained this time upwards of thirty
thousand; and, although his antagonist was
supported by Orleanists as well as Legitimists,
he beat him by no greater majority than nine
thousand. Of course, ample enough to decide
the immediate issue. Yet a comparison of
numbers within the space of little more than
one year proves the rapid growth of free
opinion in the least favourable soil of Brittany,
while a dissection of the voting as between
town and country shows that even in that
church-benighted province the monarchical
and sacerdotal influences are refiuent from
the cities and sent to stagnate and rot in the
villages.
Of the half-dozen Republican successes that
in the Gironde appears the most remarkable.
In the first place, it is a reversal of the elec-
tion of 1871. Bordeaux, the capital of the
department, is not now, perhaps, more
decidedly antipathetic to kingship of all kinds
than it was then, but, if so, it must, in the
meantime, have inoculated the district more
deeply with its proclivities; for, although the
Legitimist masters of vineyards along the
banks of the Gironde brought up their tenants
in droves at the beginning of last year and
carried their man, they have this time been
soundly beaten by their adversaries, after
having first humbled themselves to an extent
which must make their mortification infi-
nitely bitter. Despairing of a candidate of
their own colour, they stooped to unite
with Orleanists and even Imperialists, upon a
Bonapartist, who, though he put on the skin
of a Conservative and assumed the voice of a
free trader, was not able to command much
more than half the number of votes enthusi-
astiellay given to his so-called " Gambettist "
opponent.

These successes are not simply victories in
themselves; but they have a bearing upon the
whole representation of the Republic, which it is
important to take into account. A whole De-
partment votes in the filling up of a single
vacancy. It is assumable, therefore, that the
45,000 votes now given to
,34, CDUC, and
the 29,000 scraped together by M. DE FOIL-
CA.DE Li ROWETTE, show to the sitting mem-
bers for the Gironde their probable chance of
re-election on a dissolution of the present
Assembly. Their only prospect of re-election
lies in the amount of proprietary influence
which they can put into persuasive exercise ;

for it would need more local knowledge than
any Englishman possesses to form a reliable
estimate of the comparative chances of such a
powerful proprietor as the Duke DECAZES, and
an Imperialist mongrel like this year's rejected
candidate.

One thing is obvious, however, that what is
true of one Department is true of all the rest,
as to the indicative character of these single
departmental elections. The whole half-dozen
were, till now, represented entirely, as we
understand, by anti-Republicans. Those six
knots of members will now have each a Repub-
lican colleague. Will the same Departments,
at the next general election, turn quite round
and send up to the capital Republican repre-
sentatives, and such only? Perhaps it were too
much to calculate upon a revolution so com-
plete, though, on the face of present facts,
the tendency of things goes clearly in
that direction. We should but confuse the
minds of readers with particulars by going
further into the detail of these important
manifestations of the growth and direction of
Erench opinion und feeling. Nor will we em-
barrass ourselves by affecting to weigh diver-
sities betwixt TIIIERSISM and GA.MBETTAISM,
Conservative Republicanism and Republican-
ism that is Radical. The hard necessities
under which Priest and proprietor, Legitimist
and Orleanist, Imperialist and Royalist, are
driven to coalesce in order to obtain a chance
of success, will show to Republicans of all
shades, voluntary or in spite of themselves,
the wisdom of united action. Their success
will, at least, have this value above any that
their opponents can command, that MR. TIIIERS
and GAMBETTA, as representative men, will
not have that difficulty of sharing the spoils
between them which would hamper their mot-
ley adversaries beyond hope.

THE CONSERVATIVE PROGRAMME.

THERE has been a great Conservative
demonstration in East Surrey, and the
speeches delivered there are really worth
reading. Every gentleman who spoke was
angry with the Government for something or
other, most frequently for the last thing that
had turned up in the columns of the news-
papers. But the funniest part of the matter
was the way in which speaker after speaker
tried to define:the principles and programme of
their party. Mr. TALBOT, M.P., was effusive
on the Church; when he spoke of the
bishops' veneration and pathos went hand in
hand; and when, turning from this touching
subject to notice with horror that Mr. Mia Ll.
dwelt in the neighbourhood where the meeting
was held, indignation, mingled with melan-
choly, subdued the speaker, and brought him
sadly to his seat. Mr. HA.RDINGE GIFFARD,
Q.C., also did battle for the Church, and
recommended his audience to look for the pro-
gramme of the Conservatives in J. S. MILL'S
recent letter on the subject of revolution. His
attack on the Administration was unique of
its kind. " The present Government," said
the learned gentleman, "had introduced prin-
ciples into society which tended to the destruc-
tion of freedom and religion, and they had
taught people to look to this or that institu-
tion next to be despoiled, and when that was
gone to some other." The clearness of Con-
servative thought in this extract is truly
remarkable. Mr. CHARLEY, M.P., insisted that
criticism was the only duty of the Conserva-
tives. If so, it must be confessed that they
exhibit more zeal than skill in its performance.
Mr. MORGAN HOWARD called the return of
Mr. WATNEY for East Surrey a "brilliant
success,' and assured the world by a sort of
mysterious aside that "the time. was fast ap-
proaching
,when Conservatives would be able to
place before the country a definite policy which
would command its admiration. Mr. WATNEY,
the member for East Surrey, when his turn
came, as the Americans say, "spread himself
out," and delivered a scathing criticism on the
conduct of the Radical party, and hinted that
the approaching Radical policy would over-
throw the " Throne and the Constitution. On
the whole, Mr. WATNEY did not make quite a
" brilliant Success" hi his speech. The policy
of his party, he said, was "the conservation
Of the institutions of the country, and espe-
ciially of the union between Church and. State."
We know of nothing comparable to the I

Nov. 2, 1872.

utterances of our Conservative politicians for
intelligibility and clearness of thought, except,
perhaps, FOOTE'S account of the Grand Pali'
jandrum. "So she went into the garden to
cat a cabbage-leaf to make an apple pie; and,
at the same time, a great she-bear, ooming up
the street, pops its head into the shop.
What! no soap? So he died and she very
imprudently married the barber; and there
were present the Pieuinnies, and the Job-
fillies, and the Garynlies, and the Grand
Panjandrum himself, with the little round
button at top, and they all fell to playing the
game of catch as catch can, till the gunpowder
ran out at the heels of their boots." This is
very like a Conservative programme as out-
lined by leading men of the party, by the
grand Panjandrums. Whether the PiOUillllie!3
and Joblillies of the party, which, no doubt,
are a kind of operative Conservives, will be
satisfied with this much longer will some day
be discovered. In the meantime, we say, with
CHRISTOPHER SLY, "pallet's pallabris. Let
the world slide."

THE NATIONAL EDUCATION LEAGUE.
The annual meeting of the League is announced
to he held on Tuesday next at the Masonic-hall,
Birmingham. A circular issued to the members
explains the arrangements for the meeting :—The
proceedings will be opened at eleven o'clock on
Tuesday morning, by an address from the Chair-
man of the Council, Mr. George Dixon, M.P. The
report of the Executive Committee for the past
year will be then read, after which the meeting
will proceed to the election of Council, officers.,
and executive committee. A resolution will
proposed, confirmatory of the recommendations of
the executive committee contained in the circular
of the 19th of January, 1872. A motion will also
be submitted to this meeting, requesting ?sr.
Dixon to introduce into the House of Commons
early next session a resolution to the effect that
no amendments of the Elementary Education Act
will be considered satisfactory which do not pro-
vide for universal compulsion, School Boards in
all districts, and the unconditional repeal of the
25th section. A public meeting will be held in the
Town-hall in the evening, which will he addressed
by members of Parliament and other visitors at-
tending the meeting.

THE WORKING MEN'S PEACE ASSO-
CIATION.
The Council of the Working Men's International
Peace Association are making arrangements for
the prosecution of an active campaign for the fur-
therance of the principles of the association in the
provinces. It was decided to hold meetings in
Brighton, Portsmouth, Southampton, Winchester,
Salisbury, and Derby amongst other places. It is
announced that on the 26th November, a confer-
ence of representative men favourable to the prin-
ciples of peace, and international arbitration, will
be held in Manchester, for the purpose of deciding
upon the best mode of propagating peace prin-
ciples, and chiefly as to what steps were tho best
to take to commence and prosecute an active cam-
paign in the northern counties. The association
will celebrate its second anniversary, by a soil*
at the Arundel Hall, Arundel-street, Strand, on
Tuesday next. Mr. Edmond Beales will preside,
and amongst others who will take part in the pro-
ceedings are Professor Thorold Rogers and Karl
Blind.

articles.text:
RELIGIOUS'ACCOMMODATION IN LARGE

TOWNS.

In the absence of an official religious eenstni,
Mr. Mall has for his own purpose undertaken to
furnish statistics of the" religious accommodation'
in all the considerable towns of England and
Wales. So far, we have only the returns relating'
to the towns with a population of more th,aa
00,000—namely, Birmingham, Bradford, Bristol,
Brighton, Hull, Leeds, Liverpool, ilancheittere
Newcastle, Portsmouth, Salford, Sheffield, Stoke.
on. Trent, and Wolverhampton. The information

has been collected by competent persons, and
there is no reason whatever to doubt the perfect
good faith with which they have done their work.
The net result of the inquiry may be thus
stated :—ln the 14 towns named, the non-esta-
blished churches provide 584 places of worship
and 207,294 sittings more than the Established
Church, the actual -proportion of acconamodatiou
to population being 591 per cent. by the former
ad 40.2 per cent. by the latter. Comparing 1872
with 1851, it is found that in eight of the towns
Dissent has, in the matter of church extension,
outstripped the favoured communion. The six in
which the Church has increased its sitting accom-
modation beyond the Nonconformist proportion are.
Manchester, Salford, Birmingham, Leeds, Brighton,
and Hull.
The following is the relative proportion of
accommodation supplied in the fourteen towns by
theprincipal denominations :—Church of England,
427,592 sittings; Wesleyans, 142,346 ; Congre-
gationalists, 114,516 ; Baptists, 70,201; Primitive
Methodists, 46,179; United Methodists, 42,620;
Roman Catholics, 57,101. Mr. Miall has proved
much by these figures- • ,

ELECTORAL. REFORM.
A Conference on Electoral Reform, convened by
the Electoral Reform Association, will be held in
St. James's-hall, on 12th November next, The
proceedings will be opened at 12 o'clock by the
chairman, Mr. josephChamberlain, of Birmingham.
The following resolutions will be proposed by the
committee :--
1. That it is desirable to assimilate the county
and borough franch' ise whatever basis cif qualifi-
cation may be adopted.
2. That such a readjustment of constituencies
should be effected as would make the number of
electors in any one constituency approximately
equal to the number in any other.
Notice has been given to submit other resolu-

articles.title: EPPING FOREST.
articles.text:
EPPING FOREST.

Mr. Wood, Q.C., Mr. Locke, M.P., and Mr.
Watlington, the Commissioners appointed under
the Epping Forest Preservation Act, met on Wed-
nesday morning, at 6, Old Palace-yard, in order
to hear the first application under the Act of last
session, to prevent the: destruction of Part of the
trees in the Forest. Mr. Nelson, 'who appeared
on behalf of the Commissioners of Sewers, said it
was sought to restrain the injurious cutting of the
trees, under colour of what was known as the
right of estover ; but proper pruning would not be
interfered with. Mr. Merriman, on behalf of the
two persons against whom the interlocutory in-
junction was sought, expressed their willingness
to abide by the order of the Court. Mr. Smith
and Mr. Lawrence argued respectively, on behalf
of the Metropolitan Board of Works and the
Office of Public Works, that the Court had the
power to make an injunction; and ultimately
judgment was given restraining any injurious
lopping over lands which were forestal, or subject
to common rights, within the last twenty years.

articles.title: REPRESENTATION OF LABOUR
articles.text:
THE REPRESENTATION OF LABOUR

On Tuesday evening, Oot. Nth, a nume-
rous audience assembled at the rooms of the
London Patriatio Society, to hear an address
from R. Marsden Latham, Esq., President of
the Labour Representation League, on the
representation of labour. The lecturer briefly
sketched the objects and principles of the
league, and in an able manner pointed out the
evils arising from the present system of re-
presentation, and argued that until working
men, or men who understood the interests of
labour were returned to the House, the work-
ing classes would remain in their present un-
satisfactory condition. He also pointed out
the principles which, if carried out, would
benefit their condition, and concluded by
urging them to organize and unite in order to
return men of their own order to the next
House of Commons.
An animated discussion ensued, in which
Messrs. Radford, Eocariug, Boon, Mottershead,
and Harriss took part, and a cordial vote of
thanks to the lecturer and chairman closed
the meeting.

MR, OITIOFIESTER
_FORTESCUE ON

EDUCATION.

Mr. Chiebester Fortescue delivered the
opening address of the season at the Radstock
Working Men's Hall on Monday night. The
right hon. gentleman, in urging upon his
audience the importance of the cultivation of
the intellect, dwelt upon the absolute money
value of general intelligence in the working
man, down even to the humblest class of
manual labourers. The tendency of things at
present was, he said, to raise the wages of the
working classes aud to increase their leisure
by shortening their working hours, and after
referring to the enormous sums of money spent
by working men upon ,intoxicating drinks,
tobacco, and other luxuries' he put it to his
hearers whether they would make use of the
advantages which they would probably now
enjoy, to some degree, at all events, for the
purpose of increasing their intelligence and
improving their minds, or whether they would
use it for the purpose of decreasing those ad-
vantages. Speaking on the education question
generally, Mr. Forteseue :said he kad wine to
the conclusion that it would be neeosaary to
take universally, before very long, the -bold
step of compelling every parent to have his
children educated, so far, of course, as the
rudiments of education go, sufficient to save a
boy or girl from savagery and to lay the foun-
dation of future improvement. He did not see
how else they could break through the barriers
of habit and indifference which they haw shown
by many people on this subject of education.
There were other most difficult problems which
the State would have to solve, but he was sure
the State and the men who are bent upon for-
warding education would have to exhibit great
patience and strengh, and regard for the feel-
ings of others. There are (the right hon.
gentleman said) such things as short cuts
which are the longest way round, and I have
no faith in that kind of government which
may be described as enlightened and bene-
volent despotism, but the heat of things', iii-
eluding the culture of the mind of the people,
must not be forced upon them without due
regard to their feelings, and especially to their
religious feelings.

articles.title: IIYMN TO OLD OCEAN.
articles.text:
IIYMN TO OLD OCEAN.

Roll softly, Ocean, o'er thine ancient bed,
So long unclaimed by any power but thee
No longer Hit in pride thy hoary head,
Or toss thy locks in wild, unconquered glee—
Thou haat at length been conquered, oh, thou
Sea.

Down, down, beneath thy darkest, deepest wave,
Where ever-brooding stillness reigns serene—
Far, far,below the seaman's nameless grave,
'Mid coral stems and jewels' sparkling sheen,
A strange, dal k, gliding form is dimly soon!
The monster shapes thy restless deep supplies
Play their huge gambols round the slender
thing,
And start—and stare—with wild, uncouth sur-
prise,
When from its magic touch they upward spring,
And dreadful belle wings make thine arches ring!
Hush, hush thine awful thunders, sounding Sea I
Oh! cradle softly on thy mighty breast
This child of Science we intrust to thee—
Ah ! lull it gently to eternal rest,
Nor break the bond that makes two nations
bless'd !
Ay—hush thy thunders—for "the still, small
voice"
That whispers to us from thy secret caves,
And bids our heart-strings tremble or rejoice,
Is louder than thy fiercest mountain-waves,
When round our shores the roaring tempest
raves.

No more shall pining wife or mother wait
The bark's slow passage, for the welcome word
That tells her anxious ear the happy fate
Of darling son, or honoured, absent lord—
Swift as the lightning's flash this cord shall speak,
And call the flush of youth to faded cheek !
The same sweet Power that whispered, "Peace,
be still !"
When thy rude dashings touched His sacred
feet,
Has bent even thee, old Ocean, to His
And caused "the ends of earth" in joy to
meet ;
Praise to His holy name! we can no more,
But bow our heads in silence—and adore!
ANON.
